One customer's script sends 10,000 requests a minute and slows everyone. A per-customer limit of 100 per minute with a polite 'slow down' message protects others while that customer is told how to fix it.
What would you do if AI latency is too high for a voice assistant?

For a voice assistant I'd stream speech and responses, use smaller or faster models, process at the edge, keep answers short, run steps in parallel and use brief acknowledgements while thinking. I'd target well under a second to start responding, so the conversation feels natural.
In a voice call, a 5-second pause feels broken. You stream the reply so speech starts after about half a second, use a fast small model, and keep answers short.
When is it worth paying for a bigger or reasoning model?

When errors are costly and the task is complex, like a legal clause review, a bigger or reasoning model pays off. For simple work it doesn't. I'd prove the value on evals, and spend only where it pays.

Reviewing a 100-page contract for hidden penalty clauses: a missed clause is costly, so a stronger model or a reasoning model is worth the extra cost. For tagging support tickets, a small model is fine.
How would you handle an offline batch job that processes 5 million documents with an LLM?

For five million documents I'd use batch APIs, a queue and workers, chunking, idempotent retries, progress tracking and a cost estimate from a sample, with quality sampling along the way. It finishes reliably within budget.
Five million old documents must be summarised. You send them through a batch queue with many workers, retry failed ones safely (without duplicates), and show a progress bar: '3.2M of 5M done'.
What would you do if the provider silently updates the model and quality changes?
I'd pin model versions, run regression evals regularly, monitor quality metrics, and plan migrations with tests. If a provider updates silently, the monitors catch it and we respond.

A provider quietly updates its model and your invoice-extraction accuracy drops from 96% to 89%. By pinning a specific model version and running tests weekly, you catch it and upgrade only when ready.
When should you fine-tune instead of using RAG or prompting?

A legal-tech client wants every contract summary in a fixed house style, and long prompts still drift. I'd ask what's missing: facts, which RAG fixes; instructions, which better prompting fixes; or behaviour such as consistent style, format or a narrow skill, which fine-tuning can fix. I'd prove the gap on an eval set first, estimate data needs, cost and the work of redoing it when the base model changes. Most teams save time and money by trying the cheaper options first.
A legal firm wants every summary in the same house style. Long prompts still drift, so you fine-tune on 1,000 approved summaries. For 'what does the current policy say', RAG is still the better tool.
Customer asks "can we train the model on our data?" What do you say?

When a customer says "can you train the model on our data?", I'd ask why. If they want it to know their documents, RAG is usually cheaper, current and permissioned. If they want a particular style or format, prompting or fine-tuning may do it. If they're worried about privacy, we can offer contractual no-training terms or a private deployment. I'd propose a pilot with an eval set to compare. The customer gets what they need, often faster and cheaper than training.

A customer asks 'Can we train the model on our data?' You first ask why. If they want it to answer from their documents, RAG does that without retraining; if they need a particular style, fine-tuning may help.
How do you prepare a dataset for fine-tuning?

I'd select high-quality examples, such as good resolutions and approved replies, remove personal data and duplicates, balance topics, format as input-output pairs, add hard edge cases, split into train, validation and test sets, and have experts review a sample. Quality beats quantity: a smaller clean set often outperforms a large noisy one.
For a fine-tune you pick 2,000 resolved support replies that managers approved, strip names and card numbers, fix inconsistent formats, and hold out 200 examples to test on afterwards.
What are LoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning?

Full fine-tuning is expensive. LoRA and similar methods train small add-on parameters instead of all the weights, which is cheaper and faster, and the adapters can be swapped per customer or task. That means customisation with lower cost and easier versioning.
Instead of retraining a model with billions of settings, LoRA trains a small add-on (like a clip-on lens) for your task. That is cheaper, faster, and you can keep one add-on per client.
What is catastrophic forgetting?

It's when training heavily on new data makes the model worse at things it knew. For example, tuned for legal text, it gets poorer at general questions. I'd use gentler learning rates, parameter-efficient methods, mix in general data and test on broad regression sets.

A model fine-tuned on legal text gets very good at contracts but starts forgetting how to write a friendly email. That loss of earlier skills is catastrophic forgetting; mixing in general examples limits it.
How do you evaluate a fine-tuned model?

I'd compare it against the base model with good prompting on a held-out test set, add human review, safety and regression tests, and compare cost and latency, including edge cases. A model that looks better in demos has to prove it on evidence.

You test the fine-tuned model against the original with a well-written prompt, on 200 unseen examples, plus a human check for safety. It wins on style but not on accuracy, so you decide if it's worth the cost.
What are the trade-offs of fine-tuning versus using synthetic data?

Synthetic data from another model is cheap and covers rare cases, but it can copy the generator's mistakes and lack diversity. I'd use it to augment, validate with humans, and always test on real data.
You need examples of rare fraud cases, so an AI generates 5,000 fake ones. They're cheap but can copy the generating AI's mistakes, so you mix them with real cases and have an expert review a sample.
How do you decide between an LLM API and an open-source self-hosted model?

I'd compare quality on our tasks, privacy and compliance needs, cost at expected volume, latency, operations capability, support and lock-in. I'd start with an API for speed and move to open models when scale, privacy or customisation justify it.
A hospital must keep patient data on its own servers, so it chooses an open-source model it runs itself. A startup testing an idea quickly uses an API: faster to start and strongest quality.
What is distillation?
Distillation trains a smaller model to imitate a larger one's outputs, keeping much of the quality at lower cost and latency. I'd check licence terms and test on our tasks.
A giant model answers 10,000 support questions well. You train a much smaller model to copy those answers. It's 10 times cheaper to run and nearly as good on that one job.
When would you use a small language model?

A small language model fits focused tasks like classification, extraction and simple chat, or places that need privacy, offline use, low latency or low cost, like a mobile app. I'd test its limits first.
A phone app that sorts messages into 'urgent' or 'not urgent' and must work offline uses a small model on the device: cheap, private and fast enough for a narrow task.
What is a preference-tuned or RLHF model, in plain words?
It means the model was further trained using human or AI preferences about which answers are better, which makes it more helpful and polite. It shapes style and behaviour but doesn't guarantee truth.
A raw model might answer rudely. After people rate answers ('this one is clearer and kinder') and the model is tuned toward the preferred style, it becomes more helpful and polite.
What would you do if a fine-tuned model memorised sensitive training data?
I'd stop using it, assess exposure, remove sensitive data, retrain, add output filters, test extraction attacks, and follow breach rules if they apply. The prevention is sanitising training data.
Testing shows a fine-tuned model can repeat a customer's phone number from its training data. You stop using it, remove those records, retrain, and add filters and extraction tests before relaunch.
How do you avoid vendor lock-in with models?

I'd put an abstraction layer or gateway between our product and the model, keep prompts and evals portable, store our own data and embeddings, test alternatives periodically and negotiate terms. Switching then becomes realistic.
Your app calls one vendor directly in 40 places. If prices rise, switching is painful. A gateway in the middle and prompts and tests stored in your own repository let you swap vendors in days.
How would you test a new model before switching?
I'd run our eval set, compare cost and latency, shadow some traffic, canary with rollback, and monitor user metrics. A safe migration means evidence before everyone is switched.
Before moving to a new model, you run your test questions on both, compare cost and speed, shadow it on real traffic without showing answers, then release to 5% of users with a rollback.
What is prompt versioning and why do it?

Prompts are code. I'd keep them in version control with IDs, link each to eval results, release with review and rollback, and log which version produced each output. Otherwise changes become confusing and untraceable.
On Monday someone edits the prompt to be 'more concise' and refund answers get worse. With prompts in version control tied to test scores, you see the change, compare, and roll back in minutes.
Design a RAG assistant over a company's internal documents (millions of docs, per-user permissions).

Say a 20,000-person company wants "ask anything" over wikis, PDFs and tickets, but salary and legal files must stay private. I'd start by clarifying users and the top questions, then walk the pipeline: connectors, parsing, chunking with metadata and access controls, a hybrid index, a permission filter at query time, reranking, and an LLM answer with citations and an "I don't know" fallback. I'd add freshness sync, caching and observability, evaluate with recall@k, faithfulness and leak tests, and roll out department by department. Employees get cited answers from documents they may see, and security can audit every access.

A 20,000-person company asks 'What is the parental leave policy?' The system verifies who asked, searches only documents they may read, picks the best passages, answers with links, and logs who saw what.
Design an enterprise support agent (tickets, knowledge base, account data).

For a retailer's support team across email, chat and an order system, I'd design an agent that resolves common issues and escalates safely. Parts: an intent classifier, a knowledge-base RAG, tools like order lookup and refunds within limits, policy checks, escalation with summaries, and a human console. Guardrails: authentication, refund caps, approvals for exceptions. I'd measure resolution rate, CSAT, escalation quality and cost per ticket. Easy cases close without humans, hard ones reach people with context, and risk stays bounded.

A customer writes 'Where is my order #4821?' The agent checks the order system (shipped, due Friday), replies, and offers a refund only within limits. An angry customer or a high-value case goes to a human with a summary.
Design an end-to-end batching system for LLM queries and reason about latency and cost.

I'd separate traffic by urgency. Interactive requests need low latency, so small or no batches and streaming. Near-real-time work can wait a short queue window. Overnight jobs use large batches and discounted batch APIs. I'd add a queue with priorities and rate limits, dynamic or continuous batching on self-hosted servers, retries and idempotency, and measure p95 latency, throughput and cost per thousand requests. Interactive users stay fast while background work gets much cheaper.
Chat questions go straight through and stream. At night, 100,000 summaries go into big batches at a lower price. Separate queues stop big jobs slowing a user waiting for a chat reply.
Design the system for Perplexity-style answer search.

An analyst wants answers with sources, not ten blue links, and needs fresh facts that a model alone doesn't know. I'd build a pipeline: understand and rewrite the query, search the web or an index with hybrid retrieval, fetch and clean pages, chunk and rerank, then give the top passages to an LLM that writes a short answer with numbered citations. A verification step checks each citation really supports its claim. I'd stream the answer, cache popular queries, support follow-ups, score source quality and set policies for abuse and copyright. I'd measure citation accuracy, answer correctness, time to first token and cost per query. Users get a quick answer they can verify in one click.

A user asks 'What did the central bank decide today?' The system searches the web, reads the top five pages, has the model write a short answer with numbered sources [1][2], and checks each claim matches a source.
Walk me through the backend architecture of an AI product.

I'd explain it as one request travelling through boxes: the client app, an API gateway for auth and rate limits, an orchestration service that assembles the prompt, memory, retrieval and tool routing, vector store and databases, model serving through a hosted API or our own GPUs, safety filters before and after the model, then logging, evals, billing and monitoring. I'd mark latency and cost at each step. A new engineer sees where quality, cost and safety are controlled.

Describe one question's journey: the app sends it, the gateway checks login and limits, the orchestrator fetches documents, the model writes the answer, safety checks run, the answer streams back, and logs record the cost.
Design an AI agent for a streaming service.

Viewers spend ten minutes browsing and give up, so the agent's job is to get them to something to watch fast. It would recommend by mood or time available, answer "where can I watch X," manage the watchlist and handle simple support, using tools for catalogue search, recommendations, watchlist and account help, plus taste signals. Guardrails: age ratings, and no account changes without confirmation, with fallback to normal browsing. I'd measure time to first play, completion rate, satisfaction, opt-outs and cost per session.
A viewer says 'something funny, under an hour.' The agent checks their history, filters to short comedies on their services, shows three choices with reasons, and learns from what they click.
Design an AI product for a ride-sharing app.

Riders complain about unclear fares and long pickups. I'd weigh candidates, ETA prediction, matching, dynamic pricing, safety monitoring, a support agent, and pick one by impact and data readiness, say ETA accuracy. I'd define inputs such as GPS, traffic and history, a model with a fallback, how to show uncertainty, "5 to 8 min," plus A/B tests and fairness checks across areas. I'd measure ETA error, cancellations and rider satisfaction.

A rider sees 'Fare: ₹180-220' and an honest pickup time. The system estimates arrival time, matches the nearest driver with the best fit, and explains surge pricing ('High demand, +1.4x') instead of hiding it.
Design a feed ranking model (for example Instagram or a Google news feed).

Users miss posts they care about while viral posts crowd the feed. I'd generate candidates, then rank with a model predicting like, comment, share and hide probabilities, combined into a value score, plus freshness, diversity and creator-fairness rules, cold-start handling and an exploration slot. I'd evaluate offline with AUC and NDCG, then A/B test time spent, sessions, hides and surveys, with integrity filters. The aim is long-term satisfaction, not clickbait.
A user follows 300 accounts. The system picks 500 candidate posts, ranks them by predicted interest (like, reply, skip), mixes in variety, and limits repeats, so the feed isn't only viral posts.
Design the recommendation engine for Amazon's homepage, and define its success metrics.

Shoppers see a generic page and miss products they'd buy. I'd generate candidates with item-to-item collaborative filtering, recent views and trending, then rank with a model predicting click and purchase probability, apply business rules like stock, margin and diversity, handle cold-start via popularity and content features, cache for latency and keep an exploration slot. Success metrics: conversion, revenue per visit, click-through, diversity, returns and long-term repeat purchase, with latency and fairness to sellers as guardrails, validated with A/B tests. Pages become more relevant and conversion rises.
A shopper who bought a camera sees lenses and memory cards on the homepage. Success is measured by clicks and purchases, but also by returns and whether people keep coming back.
Design a Text-to-SQL assistant over a warehouse with thousands of tables.

I'd avoid pointing the model at 3,000 raw tables. First build a semantic layer of curated tables, metric definitions and descriptions. Then retrieve only the relevant schema, generate SQL, validate it with a parser, run it read-only with row and cost limits, show the SQL and results, and ask a clarifying question when the request is ambiguous. I'd evaluate on a question set with known-correct queries. Analysts get trustworthy answers and can inspect the query.

A manager asks 'Revenue by region last quarter?' The system looks at a curated 'sales' table and a metric called 'revenue' defined once, writes a query, shows the result and the query so it can be checked.
Design an AI coding agent.

A developer wants "fix this bug from the ticket." The agent indexes the repository, plans, reads and edits files, runs tests in a sandbox, and verifies with tests before proposing a small diff for review. I'd limit permissions and steps, and measure merge rate and revert rate on real tasks. Developers review small verified diffs, not untested suggestions.
A developer says 'fix the login bug in this ticket.' The agent reads the code, writes a fix, runs the tests in a sandbox, shows the changes for approval, and never merges without a human.
Design a real-time voice AI agent.

For a restaurant voice-ordering system I'd stream speech-to-text into a dialogue manager or LLM with tools for the menu and order, then stream text-to-speech back, handling interruptions and noise. The latency budget is about a second, with fallback to a human and order confirmation. I'd measure order accuracy, completion rate and latency. Customers speak naturally and the order is right.

A diner says 'Two margherita pizzas, no onions.' Speech is turned into text as they talk, the assistant confirms 'Two margherita, no onions, correct?', and replies in under a second, allowing interruptions.
Design a content moderation system using AI.

I'd use layers: rules and hashes for known bad content, ML classifiers by category, an LLM for nuance, confidence thresholds, human review queues, appeals, policy versioning and audit logs. I'd measure precision and recall by category and language, and time to action. Humans focus on cases the AI is unsure about.
A post goes through layers: a blocklist catches known illegal images, a classifier flags hate speech, an AI reviews borderline cases, and uncertain or severe ones go to trained human moderators.
Design a personalised recommendation system with AI.

A streaming service wants a personalised home page. I'd use candidate generation, collaborative and content-based, then a ranking model with user and context features, business rules, diversity and freshness, cold-start handling, a feedback loop and A/B tests. I'd measure watch time, retention and diversity, so users find relevant content and the team can show real impact.
Maya watches thrillers on weekends. The home page finds candidate shows from viewers like her, ranks them for her evenings, mixes in a few new genres, and avoids repeats.
Design an AI-powered search for an e-commerce platform.

For an online store with poor search conversion, I'd add query understanding (spelling, synonyms, intent), hybrid retrieval, learning-to-rank from clicks and purchases, personalisation and filters, and maybe conversational search. I'd evaluate with NDCG, null-result rate and conversion. Shoppers find items faster and revenue rises.
A shopper types 'runing shoes for flat feet'. The search fixes the spelling, understands the intent, ranks suitable shoes on top, and shows filters like size and price.
Design a multimodal search system (text, image, video).

To search videos by describing a scene, I'd embed text, images and video frames into a shared space, index with metadata, combine with keyword search, rerank, and manage latency and storage. I'd evaluate with relevance judgments.

A user types 'a dog catching a frisbee at sunset'. The text and the video frames are turned into numbers in the same space, so the system finds clips whose content matches, even with no matching words.
Design an LLM evaluation platform.

Teams build LLM features with no shared testing, so I'd build a platform with dataset management, versioned prompts, runners for models, scoring by rules, LLM judges and humans, dashboards, regression gates in CI, production sampling and access control. All teams get consistent quality gates.
Three teams each test prompts in spreadsheets. A shared platform stores datasets, runs the same tests on any prompt, shows scores side by side and blocks releases that fall under the bar.
Design an AI gateway for managing LLM access across an organisation.

I'd provide one entry point with authentication, routing across models, rate limits and budgets, caching, logging, PII filters, guardrails, fallbacks and analytics. The company gets control, savings and safety.

Instead of 12 teams each calling AI vendors with their own keys, they call one internal gateway that logs usage, applies budgets, blocks sensitive data, and switches to a backup model if the first is down.
Design memory for a personal AI assistant.

I'd store facts with consent, summarise conversations, retrieve relevant memories, and let users view, edit and delete them, with expiry for stale items and no sensitive storage by default. I'd evaluate recall and harm. The assistant feels personal but stays controllable.
A personal assistant remembers 'I'm vegetarian' only because the user agreed. It stores that fact, brings it up when ordering food, and the user can view it, edit it or delete it in settings.
Design a deep research agent.

I'd plan sub-questions, search and read sources in parallel, extract notes with citations, cross-check them, synthesise a report and state limits. I'd budget steps and cost, verify sources and evaluate quality. Analysts get a cited report with controlled cost.

Asked 'Is the EV battery market consolidating?', the agent breaks it into questions, reads 30 sources in parallel, takes notes with citations, cross-checks contradictions, and writes a report with a source list.
Design a multi-tenant chatbot platform where each business gets a custom bot.

Each business needs a custom bot on shared infrastructure, so I'd isolate tenant data and prompts, give each a knowledge base, provide a configuration UI, quotas, versioning and analytics, and keep security tight. That makes customisation scalable and safe.
A platform hosts bots for a bakery and a law firm. Each bot sees only its own documents and prompt, has its own rate limit and bill, and one tenant's traffic spike doesn't slow the other.
Design an AI meeting summariser handling thousands of meetings daily.

For thousands of meetings daily: transcription, speaker labels, chunking for long meetings, summaries and action items with timestamp citations, privacy controls, queued processing and quality evaluation. Users get reliable notes at scale.
A 90-minute meeting is transcribed, labelled by speaker, split into sections, and summarised with action items ('Ravi: send quote by Friday'). A queue handles thousands of meetings an hour.
Design an AI document-processing pipeline for a financial institution.

For a bank's loan documents: ingestion, OCR and layout parsing, classification, field extraction with validation, confidence thresholds, human review, audit trail and security. I'd measure field accuracy and the share processed with no human touch. The bank processes faster with controlled errors.
A bank receives a scanned loan file. The system reads the text (OCR), recognises the document type, extracts income and name, checks the numbers add up, and sends doubtful ones to a human reviewer.
Design an AI resume screening system handling 100K applications a week.

With 100,000 applications a week, I'd parse resumes, match them to criteria, rank with explanations, audit for bias, keep humans deciding, offer appeals and log everything. I'd measure recall of qualified candidates and fairness, so screening is efficient and defensible.

100,000 applications arrive a week. The system extracts skills, matches them to the job's criteria, ranks with reasons, audits results for bias across groups, and keeps a recruiter making the final call.
Design a fraud detection system with LLM support.

For a payments company, I'd use real-time ML scoring on transactions with rules, graph features and thresholds. The LLM helps investigators with summaries and case triage, and humans review. A feedback loop retrains the models. I'd measure precision, recall, the cost of false positives and latency, so fraud is caught while good customers aren't blocked.

A card payment arrives. In milliseconds a model scores risk using device, location and history. High scores are blocked, middle ones asked for a code, and an LLM summarises the case for the investigator.
Design an AI-powered email assistant.

I'd prioritise and summarise email, draft replies in the user's tone using their permissions, require confirmation before sending, add privacy controls and learn from edits. Executives save time without risky sends.
The assistant summarises the 40 unread emails, drafts a reply 'Thanks Priya, Thursday works' in the user's tone, and waits for a tap on Send. It never sends or deletes without confirmation.
Design an AI notification system that prioritises instead of broadcasting.

I'd score importance per user and context, set timing and frequency caps, choose channels, offer digests, learn from feedback and opt-outs, and A/B test on retention and complaints. Users get fewer, better alerts.
Instead of 30 pings, you get one morning digest. The system scores importance (a payment failure is urgent, a like isn't), respects quiet hours, and caps how many alerts you get per day.
Design a medical diagnosis assistant.

I'd position it as clinician support, not replacement: retrieve clinical guidelines, use patient data with consent, suggest a differential with evidence and uncertainty, require clinician review, keep audit logs, plan regulatory review and test for bias. Clinicians get safer decision support.

A doctor types a patient's symptoms. The assistant retrieves clinical guidelines, lists possible conditions with sources and confidence, flags missing tests, and the doctor decides. It never shows diagnoses to patients directly.
Design an on-device AI assistant.

For a phone assistant that works offline, I'd use small quantised models and local retrieval within battery and memory limits, with optional cloud fallback with consent, plus updates and privacy by design. It's fast and private for common tasks.

A phone assistant works on a plane. A small compressed model runs locally for simple tasks like setting alarms, stays within battery limits, and sends harder requests to the cloud only when online and allowed.
Design ChatGPT-like product end to end (at a high level).

At a high level: client apps, API gateway and auth, a conversation store, orchestration, model serving with batching and autoscaling, safety filters, tools and retrieval, memory, observability, billing and rate limits. I'd walk through one request and mark latency and cost at each step.
You type a question. The app authenticates you, loads your conversation, adds instructions, calls the model, checks safety, streams the answer back, saves the chat and records usage for billing.
Design a high-level system for an AI assistant responding to a user query.

When a user sends a query: authentication and rate limit, safety checks, context assembly from history, memory and retrieval, model call with streaming, tool calls if needed, output filtering, logging and feedback. I'd narrate that path so the interviewer sees the end-to-end flow.
User asks 'Summarise my invoice.' The system checks login and limits, screens for unsafe content, pulls the invoice and chat history, calls the model, filters the output, and streams the summary.
Design an AI tutor for students.

For a school, I'd start with learning goals and curriculum grounding, then adaptive questioning, hints instead of answers, safety for minors, teacher dashboards and evaluation by learning outcomes. Students learn and teachers stay informed.
A student answers 'x = 4' to an algebra question, which is wrong. The tutor asks a hint question instead of the answer, adapts the next problem, and shows the teacher where the class is struggling.
Design an AI data product.

A company has years of operational data and managers can't use it. I'd identify the decisions, like weekly sales risks, build a governed data layer and semantic model of metrics, add natural-language questions with visible SQL, automated insight alerts and permissions, and an eval set of real questions. Success is decisions made, time to insight and trust measured as correct answers.

A retail manager wants to know 'Which stores will run out of stock next week?' The data product pulls sales and delivery data, forecasts, and presents a short weekly list of actions rather than dashboards.
Design a demand signal engine that pulls customer feedback and shows what the product team should work on.

Feedback arrives from tickets, reviews, sales calls and surveys and nobody reads it all. I'd ingest the sources with permissions, deduplicate, tag with LLM themes and sentiment, cluster, link to customers and revenue, and rank by frequency, severity, customer value and trend, showing real quotes. A human reviews the themes, and I'd check accuracy against manual samples. PMs see a ranked, evidence-backed list.

Hundreds of comments say 'export is slow' in tickets, reviews and calls. The system gathers them, groups similar ones, counts by customer value, and shows the team 'Export speed: 142 mentions, 9 big customers'.
Design a real-time monitoring system with AI in part of it.

An ops team gets thousands of alerts, mostly noise. I'd stream metrics, logs and traces, use rules for known failures and anomaly detection for unknown ones, then let an LLM summarise an incident and propose next steps, with deduplication, routing and human approval for actions. I'd measure detection delay, false-alert rate and mean time to resolve. Engineers get fewer, richer alerts.
An ops team gets 5,000 alerts a day. Rules catch known issues, a model groups related alerts into one incident ('database slow, 40 alerts') and an assistant drafts a summary and first checks.
Design an AI summariser for an email app (like Gemini in Gmail).

An executive has 200 unread emails and ten minutes. I'd retrieve the thread, strip signatures, summarise with action items and deadlines, link to the original messages, process within the user's permissions and avoid storing content beyond need. I'd evaluate faithfulness, no invented dates, and omissions. Users trust it because it links back to the source.

An executive has 200 unread emails and ten minutes. The summariser reads each thread, ignores signatures, produces a two-line summary with 'needs your reply' flags, and links back to the original email.
Using AI, what platform would you build to resolve data discrepancies across a luxury hotel chain?

Guest names, preferences and bookings differ across reservations, spa, loyalty and front-desk systems. I'd ingest from each, resolve guests with rules plus ML matching, detect conflicts, rank source trust, propose fixes with confidence scores, require staff approval for sensitive changes and write back, with consent and privacy controls. I'd measure duplicate rate, discrepancy rate and guest satisfaction. Staff see one consistent guest profile.

A guest is 'Mr. Anil Shah' at the front desk, 'A. Shah' in the spa system and 'Anil S.' in loyalty, with different room preferences. The platform matches them as one person, picks the most recent trusted value for each field, and flags uncertain matches for staff.
If you were building autocomplete, how would you use data to predict the next word?

I'd start with a language model or n-gram model over common phrases, personalise with the user's own history on device, rank candidates, filter offensive or sensitive suggestions and keep latency in tens of milliseconds. I'd measure acceptance rate and keystrokes saved, and keep personal data local for privacy.
You type 'See you at the'. The model, trained on many sentences, predicts 'office', 'airport', 'party' and ranks them using your own past messages, so it suggests the word you actually tend to type.
Design a RAG system to help TikTok's moderators detect and handle misinformation.

Moderators need to judge viral claims quickly against reliable sources. I'd index trusted fact-checks and news with dates, extract claims from videos using transcripts and captions, retrieve evidence, and have an LLM give a verdict with sources and uncertainty, shown to moderators in queues ordered by virality, with decisions logged. It supports decisions, not automatic bans. I'd measure precision and recall against expert labels and time per case.

A moderator sees a viral post claiming 'Drinking hot water cures flu.' The system retrieves trusted health-organisation fact-checks, shows the relevant lines with links, and suggests a label, which the moderator confirms.
Design a system for a healthcare agent that summarises a patient's medical history.

A doctor has five minutes before a visit and a 200-page record. I'd gather records with consent and role-based access, extract structured facts like diagnoses, medications and allergies, and summarise with every statement linked to its source note, flagging conflicts and missing data, never inventing, with clinician review and an audit log. I'd evaluate omission and error rates with clinicians. They get a fast overview they can verify in one click.

A doctor has five minutes with a 200-page record. The assistant, allowed to see only what that doctor may see, shows a one-page timeline with sources: 'Diabetes diagnosed 2019, last HbA1c in March, allergic to penicillin'.
Design an AI tool that helps professional consumers (prosumers).

Freelancers and small-business owners need pro-level output with consumer simplicity. I'd pick one workflow, like proposals or invoicing, give templates plus AI drafting, integrate with their tools, offer free to paid upgrades on usage, and measure activation, weekly use and conversion, with trust features like edit control and data privacy.

A freelance designer wants professional invoices without learning accounting. The tool does one job well: type 'bill Acme for 3 logos', and it produces a polished invoice, sends it, and chases late payments.
How can LLMs be integrated into Rocket Money (a personal finance app)?

Users forget subscriptions and don't know where money goes. I'd add plain-English spending insights, subscription-negotiation help, bill explanations and Q&A over transactions, using structured data tools for numbers since the LLM must not compute from memory, with strict privacy, no regulated financial advice, confirmation before any action and evals on figure correctness.
A user opens the app and sees 'You pay for 3 streaming services you haven't used in 2 months (₹1,400/month). Cancel?'. An AI explains spending in plain English and drafts the cancellation email.
Vibe code a solution to help Shopify shop owners find marketplace apps.

In 60 to 90 minutes, I'd define the merchant's need, build a simple app where they describe a goal, have an LLM map it to app categories from a small catalogue, show top matches with reasons and install links, and collect thumbs feedback. I'd say what's mocked and what a production version needs: real data, evals and permissions.
A merchant types 'I need to reduce abandoned carts'. A simple prototype recommends three marketplace apps with reasons, and you test it with five real merchants to see if the suggestions make sense.
How would you approach making a deterministic workflow system more configurable and AI-enabled?

A rules-based approvals system needs engineers for every change. I'd keep deterministic core steps for compliance, then add a natural-language configuration layer that proposes workflow changes as a reviewable diff, with schema validation, test runs on historical cases, human approval and versioning. AI is used only at ambiguous steps like classification, with confidence thresholds and fallback to rules.

An approvals tool needs an engineer for each rule change. You keep the safe fixed steps (budget over $10K needs a director) and let a manager type 'also require legal review for new vendors', which the AI turns into a rule for review.
How would you improve an Azure data product using AI?

Data engineers spend hours debugging pipelines. I'd choose pipeline failure diagnosis: collect logs and lineage, have an LLM summarise root cause and suggest fixes with links, test suggestions in a safe sandbox, keep humans approving changes, and measure mean time to resolve.
A data pipeline fails at 3 a.m. The assistant reads the logs, says 'A source column was renamed from cust_id to customer_id', suggests the fix, and a data engineer approves it.
How can AI help a business intelligence team do its work better?

Analysts spend most of their time on ad-hoc requests. I'd use natural-language querying over governed metrics, auto-generated dashboards and narrative summaries, anomaly alerts, documentation generation and data-quality checks, with humans reviewing high-stakes numbers. Ticket volume drops and insight arrives faster.
An analyst gets 'revenue by region for last quarter?' ten times a day. A natural-language query tool answers the common ones from approved definitions, so analysts have time for deeper work.
How would you reduce alert fatigue in a security operations (SOC) product?

Analysts see thousands of alerts daily and miss real threats. I'd deduplicate and correlate alerts into incidents, score by risk with context like asset value and user behaviour, use ML and LLM summaries to prioritise and explain, automate low-risk triage with audit logs and collect analyst feedback. I'd measure alerts per analyst, time to triage and missed true positives using simulations.
A security analyst gets 4,000 alerts, 3,900 of them the same failed-login pattern. The product groups them into one incident, ranks it by risk, and writes a short summary with suggested next steps.
How would you design UI and UX around AI latency and multimodal features?

Users stare at a spinner for twelve seconds while an AI image or answer is generated. I'd stream text as it arrives, show progress and steps, offer partial results, let users cancel, set expectations like "about 20 seconds," preload fast defaults, handle failures with retry, show uncertainty and let users switch between voice, image and text. I'd test perceived latency in usability sessions.
An AI image takes 12 seconds. The UI shows a progress bar, a low-quality preview first, and lets the user keep working. Text streams in word by word so it doesn't feel frozen.
Critique an AI app.

I'd critique it in a structured way: the user and job, value delivered, quality with real prompt failures, UX trust cues, latency and correction, safety and privacy, business model and cost, and metrics. I'd run a few real prompts, note failures, then give three prioritised improvements with expected impact.

Critiquing a 'smart recipe app': who is it for (busy parents), what job does it do (dinner in 20 minutes), where does the AI fail (suggests ingredients they don't have), and what would you change first.
Roblox has users in many languages and an ML auto-translation system. Design a system that translates between players on different servers.

Players in Brazil and Japan chat in the same game and messages must arrive in under a second. The chat service detects language, checks a cache of common phrases, sends to a translation service, an ML model sharded by language pair, applies safety and slang filters, and returns translated text to each recipient in their language. Messages stream through a queue, latency stays around 300 ms, with fallback to the original text and feedback collection. I'd handle game slang with glossaries and evaluate with human bilinguals.
A player in Brazil types 'Vamos jogar?'. The message is translated to Japanese in under a second, cached for repeated phrases, and shown with a small 'translated' label and the original on tap.

s.t: AI strategy, metrics and product thinking
q: You own an internal AI platform that other teams build agents on. What is your strategy and what is the one metric you own?

Ten teams build agents on ten stacks and quality and cost vary. My strategy is to make the platform the easiest and safest path: treat internal builders as customers, standardise the model gateway, evals, tool and MCP registry, guardrails and observability, provide templates, reduce time to first agent and enforce safety centrally. The one metric I'd own is the number of agents in production that meet the quality bar each quarter, or time from idea to production, paired with guardrails on cost and incidents. Teams ship faster with consistent quality.

As owner of an internal AI platform you aim to have teams ship agents faster and safely. One metric you might own: 'agents live in production meeting the quality bar', because it combines adoption and trust.
How would you define success metrics for an AI-oriented feature or product?

A summarisation feature launches and the team only tracks clicks. I'd use a layered set: outcome, like task completed and time saved; quality, like accuracy, acceptance rate and edit distance; engagement, repeat use; trust and safety, complaints, hallucination rate and opt-outs; and efficiency, cost per task and latency. I'd choose a north star, add guardrails, set targets from a baseline and review by segment.

A summarisation feature tracks clicks only, which says nothing about quality. You add: share of summaries used without edit (outcome), accuracy score on a test set (quality), time saved, and complaint rate (guardrail).
How do you test a non-deterministic system?

An LLM answers "What is our refund window?" with different wording every time. I'd test behaviour and facts, not exact text. Define pass criteria as properties: correct facts, required fields present, forbidden content absent. Run each test case several times and report a pass rate and its variance. Use rubric or LLM graders calibrated against human labels, reduce randomness where possible with low temperature and structured output, and keep a regression set and production monitoring. That gives a stable quality number despite changing wording.
An AI says 'You can return within 30 days' and 'Returns are allowed for 30 days'. The wording differs, so you test the facts (does it say 30?) and rules (never promises refunds), not exact sentences.
How do you reduce false negatives and false positives in an AI product?

A fraud model blocks good customers, false positives, and misses fraud, false negatives. I'd quantify the cost of each error type, choose thresholds accordingly, analyse error clusters, improve data and features, add a second-stage review for borderline cases and monitor precision and recall by segment. Different products set different thresholds.

A fraud model blocks good customers (false positive) and misses real fraud (false negative). You count each, put a cost on each (a lost sale vs a stolen amount), and set the threshold where the total cost is lowest.
Your evaluation framework for an AI agent that resolves support tickets: before and after launch.

The agent will answer customers without a human, so before launch I'd build a golden set of historical tickets with outcomes, score correctness and policy compliance, check tool calls in a sandbox, add adversarial tests and human review, and set thresholds. Then run in shadow mode, then a canary. After launch I'd watch resolution rate, escalation precision, CSAT, repeat contacts, refund errors, cost and drift, with weekly audits of random conversations.

Before launch, you replay 500 past tickets and check the agent's answers. After launch you track: share resolved without human help, reopened tickets, customer satisfaction and cost per ticket, and review a sample weekly.
How do you decide what to automate versus keep human in the loop, and how does that line move over time?

An agent could approve small refunds, but also large ones. I'd rank tasks by impact of error, reversibility, regulation and agent accuracy. Start with suggestions, then approvals, then autonomy for low-risk tasks with monitoring and sampling. The line moves when metrics hold over time and incidents are low, and moves back if drift appears.
An agent may approve refunds under $20 on its own, because they're low-risk and reversible. Refunds over $200 go to a human. As accuracy proves out over months, the $20 limit might rise.
What methods or metrics do you use to evaluate how well your LLM performs?

A leader asks for proof the assistant is good. I'd give a layered answer: task success on a labelled set, factual accuracy and groundedness, rubric scores from humans or calibrated LLM judges, safety and refusal tests, latency, cost, user satisfaction and regression sets, with offline benchmarks on our own data first and then online A/B tests and production sampling.
A leader asks 'Prove the assistant is good.' You show: 88% task success on 300 labelled questions, 4% hallucination rate, average 2.5-second reply, and a human reviewer score from a weekly sample.
Define success metrics for a collaborative workspace inside ChatGPT.

Teams share chats and files in a workspace. I'd pick a north star of weekly active teams completing shared tasks, supported by members per workspace, shared artefacts created and reused, time to first shared output, retention by team and quality feedback, with guardrails on data-leak incidents and cost per active team.

For a shared workspace in a chat product, the north star could be 'weekly active teams that complete a task together'. Supporting metrics: invites sent, shared chats reopened, and time to first shared result.
What metrics would you track to evaluate your ML pipeline?

A recommendation pipeline silently degrades, so I'd monitor data, model and business. Data: freshness, volume, missing values and schema drift. Model: AUC, precision, recall, calibration and drift. System: latency, errors, cost and throughput. Business: conversion and retention. Add alerts and retraining triggers so problems are found before customers feel them.

A recommendation pipeline silently degrades. You'd watch data (is yesterday's data complete?), the model (accuracy on recent examples) and the business (click and purchase rates) so you spot a problem within a day.
Design an evaluation framework for ads ranking.

An ads team changes ranking and revenue rises but users complain. Offline I'd use AUC, log loss and calibration on click and conversion predictions. Online, A/B tests on revenue per session, advertiser ROI, click-through, conversion, retention, ad hides and complaints, plus long-term holdouts. I'd add fairness and fraud checks and guardrails on ad load. Changes ship only if they help advertisers, users and revenue together.

After an ads ranking change, revenue rises but users complain. Offline you check prediction accuracy; online you run an A/B test measuring revenue, ad relevance ratings, hide-ad clicks and return visits.
How would you adapt a generative AI model to perform well in a specific domain?

A legal team needs reliable contract analysis. I'd start with prompting and examples, add RAG with domain documents and a glossary, and fine-tune only if style or reasoning gaps remain. I'd build a domain eval set with experts, add guardrails and citations, and monitor.

A legal team needs reliable contract analysis. You start with prompts and examples, add retrieval of their clause library, and fine-tune only if style or accuracy is still lacking, testing on real contracts.
Develop a strategy for a model provider's fine-tuning capability using public docs.

A provider offers fine-tuning but adoption is low. I'd segment customers, like those needing consistent style or format, lower latency or cost savings from smaller tuned models, reduce friction with data-prep tools, evals and templates, clear pricing and case studies, and measure successful tuned deployments, savings and retention. I'd note data-privacy and quality risks, and verify capabilities in current public docs before presenting.

A provider's fine-tuning feature has low adoption. You find two groups: customers who need a consistent style, and those with specialised vocabulary. You then offer guides, templates and a 'try with 100 examples' trial.
How would you decide whether a problem should use AI, generative AI, an agent, traditional programming or a simple rule?

A team proposes an LLM for everything. I'd use a decision ladder. If rules are clear and stable, use code. If it's prediction from labelled data, use classic ML. If it's language, summarising or open-ended content, use generative AI. If it needs multi-step tool use with varying paths, consider an agent. Compare accuracy, cost, latency, risk and maintainability. The simplest reliable solution wins.
A team wants an LLM to decide if a number is over $100. That's a simple rule in code. Sorting messy emails by intent suits AI. Booking travel across many tools might need an agent.
Can AI be used alongside existing human and rules-based processes rather than replacing them?

Yes, and often that's the best route. A bank fearing to replace trained staff can start in assist mode with drafts, summaries and flags, run AI in shadow next to the existing process, compare results, route only low-risk cases to AI, keep rules as checks and humans for exceptions, and expand as metrics prove reliability.
A bank doesn't want to replace staff. Assist mode: the AI drafts a loan summary, a trained officer reviews and approves, and over time easy cases may be automated once results are proven.
As a PM at a model provider, build an enterprise product.

Enterprises want AI but worry about security and control. I'd define an offering for IT, security and business teams: SSO, admin controls, data privacy and no-training terms, audit logs, integrations, usage analytics, compliance certifications and reliability SLAs. Start with one high-value workflow, pilot with design partners, price per seat plus usage, and measure active seats, retention and security approvals.

An enterprise wants AI but worries about security. You package: single sign-on, admin controls, no training on their data, audit logs, and a data-residency option, sold with a pilot for one department.
How would you roll out a new feature for an answer-engine product?

A new deep-research mode costs far more per query. I'd dogfood internally, run a small beta, then a staged percentage rollout with feature flags, monitoring quality, latency, cost and abuse, setting kill criteria, comparing with control, gathering qualitative feedback and considering paid tiers for expensive modes.
A deep-research mode costs 20 times more per query. You first use it inside the company, then invite 1,000 beta users, then roll it to paying users in stages while watching cost, quality and usage.
How would you approach building proactive AI?

Users would like reminders before they ask but hate interruptions. I'd pick high-value moments with strong signals, make it opt-in, favour precision over recall, explain "why am I seeing this," make dismissal and tuning easy, cap frequency, and measure acceptance versus annoyance. Start with low-stakes suggestions.
A calendar assistant says 'You leave in 20 minutes; traffic is heavy' only before real meetings, once, with an easy 'don't show this again'. Too many pings would annoy users, so you cap alerts.
What are general applications of AI within customer support?

A support leader wants a roadmap. I'd list self-service answers, agent assist with draft replies and summaries, ticket triage and routing, sentiment and escalation detection, knowledge-base generation, QA scoring of conversations, voice bots and analytics on contact drivers, and prioritise by volume, risk and data readiness, starting with low-risk assist.
For customer support, AI can draft replies for human agents, answer common questions itself, summarise long tickets, route cases to the right team, and spot rising complaint topics.
How would you improve your favourite product with AI?

Pick a real user pain, not an AI feature looking for a problem, explain why AI beats alternatives, define the experience, risks like errors and privacy, an MVP and success metrics. For a music app, I might explain why a song was recommended and build a playlist from a described mood, with a "not this" feedback loop.
For a note-taking app, a pain is 'I can't find my old notes'. AI search by meaning fixes that better than folders. You'd define success (found in under 10 seconds) and test it on real notes.
What happens when you type a URL in the browser and press enter?

When I type a URL and press Enter, the browser checks its cache, DNS turns the name into an IP address, it opens a connection with a TLS handshake, sends an HTTP request through a CDN and load balancer to a server, which may call databases and APIs and returns a page, and the browser downloads and renders HTML, CSS, JavaScript and images. If a customer's site is slow, I can name each hop and measure where the delay sits.
You type example.com. The browser checks its cache, asks DNS for the address (93.184.x.x), connects securely, requests the page, the server replies, and the browser draws it.
What is a load balancer and what happens if it fails?

A load balancer spreads incoming requests across servers, runs health checks and stops sending traffic to broken servers, so users see one reliable address. If the load balancer itself fails, everything behind it disappears. That's why I'd run a redundant pair or a managed cloud load balancer across zones, with failover. A retailer's sale then keeps running even if one fails.
A shop uses three servers. A load balancer sends each visitor to a healthy one. If one server dies, it stops sending visitors there. If the load balancer itself dies, a second one takes over.
What is caching and what are the risks?

Caching keeps frequent results in fast memory so you avoid repeating slow work: a product page might drop from 2 seconds to 80 milliseconds. The risks are stale data, inconsistent views, a stampede when many entries expire together, and memory cost. I'd use sensible TTLs, invalidate on updates, and let only one request refill a key. A price change should show up within seconds.

A product page is read 10,000 times but changes once a day. Storing it in a cache means the database does the work once, not 10,000 times. Risk: after a price change, the cache may show the old price.
What is the CAP theorem in plain words?

CAP says that when a network split happens, a distributed system must choose between consistency, everyone sees the same latest data so some requests may be refused, and availability, always answering even if stale. Bank balances choose consistency; a like count can choose availability. I pick per feature, such as "never show a wrong balance, but a stale like count is fine."

Two bank branches lose their connection. Should they keep serving customers with possibly stale balances (availability) or refuse until reconnected (consistency)? CAP says you can't have both during the split.
What if traffic grows 10x next quarter?

Marketing says traffic will grow 10x after a big launch. I'd estimate peak requests per second and data growth, then load test to find the first bottleneck, which is often the database. I'd add caching, read replicas, queues for non-urgent work, autoscaling with limits and a CDN, set per-customer rate limits, test failover, build dashboards and alerts, write a runbook, and rehearse a week before. Launch day should look boring.

Marketing expects 10 times more traffic after a big launch. You estimate the peak at 5,000 requests a second, load test at that level, add servers and database capacity, and prepare a queue for spikes.
What happens if the cache goes down?

If the cache goes down at peak, every request hits the database and can overload it, a stampede. I'd mitigate with replicas, graceful degradation, rate limiting, request coalescing, circuit breakers and cache warm-up on recovery. The system should degrade, not collapse.

At peak the cache fails, and a million requests hit the database at once and slow it to a crawl. To protect it, you keep a second cache, limit requests reaching the database, and warm up the cache after a restart.
What is eventual consistency?

Eventual consistency means replicas converge to the same value after a short time rather than instantly. A user may update a profile and briefly see old data on another device. It improves availability and speed, and I'd design the experience and rules for it, such as making sure users see their own writes immediately.
You post a photo and your friend in another country sees the like count 3 seconds later. For a few seconds copies of the data disagree but soon match. That's fine for likes, not for bank balances.
What is database replication and what happens if the primary fails?

Replicas copy data from the primary for redundancy and read capacity. If the primary fails, I'd promote a replica automatically. The risks are data loss with asynchronous replication, split-brain and lag. I'd rehearse failovers so the outage is short and controlled.
The main database copies every change to two replicas. If the main one crashes, a replica is promoted. Some very recent writes might be lost if the copy was slightly behind.
What is sharding and why is it hard?
Sharding splits data across databases by a key such as user ID. It lets you scale, but joins, transactions, rebalancing and hot shards get harder. Choosing the shard key carefully is the hard part.
A user database is split by user ID so users 1 to 1 million are on one machine and the next million on another. It scales, but reports across all users and transfers between machines become harder.
What is a message queue and when do you use one?

A queue lets one part of a system hand work to another to be done later. If order processing slows checkout, I'd put follow-up work, emails or thumbnails in a queue. It smooths spikes, decouples services and allows retries, but it's not for steps that need an instant answer.
When someone places an order, a queue lets the email, invoice and warehouse steps happen afterwards. If email is slow, the customer still sees 'Order placed' straight away.
What happens if a message is processed twice?

Queues often deliver at least once, so duplicates will happen. I make handlers idempotent using unique IDs, deduplication tables or conditional updates, so a payment event delivered twice charges once.
A queue delivers 'charge ₹500' twice by accident. Using a unique ID per payment, the second attempt is recognised and ignored, so the customer is only charged once.
What is idempotency and why does it matter?
An idempotent operation gives the same result if repeated. If a user double-clicks Pay, an idempotency key makes the retry return the first result instead of charging twice, which makes retries safe.
A user double-clicks Pay. Both requests carry the same idempotency key, so the server charges once and returns the same result to the second request.
What is a CDN?
A CDN caches static content on servers near users, so customers in Asia see images fast and your origin carries less load. I'd set TTLs and invalidation and protect private content.
A user in Mumbai opens your site hosted in Virginia. With a CDN the images load from a server in Mumbai in 50 milliseconds instead of 300, and your main server handles less traffic.
What are the main rate-limiting algorithms?

The common ones are fixed window, sliding window, token bucket, which allows bursts, and leaky bucket, which smooths traffic. I'd apply per user, key or IP, return 429 with retry hints and keep counters in a fast shared store.
A token bucket allows 10 requests per second with bursts: a user can send 5 at once if they've been quiet. A fixed window of 100 per minute can let someone send 100 at 0:59 and 100 more at 1:00.
Horizontal versus vertical scaling?

Vertical means a bigger machine: simple but limited and a single point of failure. Horizontal means more machines: scalable and resilient but needs stateless design and load balancing. For growth I'd plan for horizontal.

Vertical scaling: buy a bigger machine for the checkout service (simple, but there's a ceiling and one machine to fail). Horizontal scaling: run ten small copies behind a load balancer and add more as needed.
What does a stateless service mean and why is it good?
A stateless service keeps no session in its own memory; state lives in shared stores. Any instance can serve any request, which makes scaling and recovery easy.
A stateless server doesn't keep your shopping cart in its own memory; it's stored in a shared store. So your next click can go to any of ten servers, and if one dies, you lose nothing.
What is a microservice architecture and what are its downsides?

Microservices allow independent deployment and scaling and clear team ownership. The downsides are network latency, harder debugging, data-consistency issues and operations overhead. Unless scale or team size demand it, I'd start with a modular monolith.

An online store splits into separate services for orders, payments and search, so each team can release on its own. The downside: more network calls, harder debugging and more moving parts to monitor.
What is a circuit breaker?

When a downstream service is failing and slowing everything, a circuit breaker opens after too many failures so calls fail fast or use a fallback, then it tests recovery. It prevents cascading failures and keeps the system responsive.
A payment provider starts failing and each call hangs for 30 seconds. After 5 failures, the circuit breaker 'opens' and returns an error instantly for a minute, instead of making users wait.
What are retries with exponential backoff and jitter?

If a service retries immediately, it can overload a recovering system. Backoff waits progressively longer, one, two, four seconds, and jitter adds randomness so clients don't retry together. I'd also cap retries.

A call fails. The system retries after 1 second, then 2, 4, 8, with a small random delay (jitter) so thousands of clients don't all retry at the same instant and knock the recovering service down again.
What is the difference between latency and throughput?

Latency is how long one request takes; throughput is how many requests per unit of time. A system can have high throughput and poor latency, so I'd track p50, p95 and p99 latency to diagnose the right problem.
A road can have low latency (a car takes 5 minutes) but low throughput (one lane, 50 cars per hour). A highway has more throughput. A system can respond fast to one user but struggle with many.
How do you define SLIs, SLOs and SLAs?

An SLI is a measured indicator, like the share of successful requests. An SLO is the internal target, say 99.9%. An SLA is the contractual promise with penalties. Error budgets help decide release pace.
SLI: 99.2% of requests succeeded this month (measured). SLO: our goal is 99.5% (internal target). SLA: we promise customers 99% or give credits (contract).
How do you design for high availability?

I'd remove single points of failure with redundancy across zones, health checks, autoscaling, graceful degradation, backups, tested failover and monitoring. The business gets fewer and shorter outages.

For high availability, run two servers in different data centres behind a load balancer, with a replicated database, health checks and an automatic switch, so one failure doesn't take the service down.
What is the difference between RPO and RTO?

RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data loss is acceptable in time. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how fast service must return. They drive backup and replication choices and their costs.
RPO: if the database crashes, losing the last 5 minutes of orders is acceptable (RPO = 5 minutes). RTO: it must be back up within 30 minutes (RTO = 30 minutes).
What happens if a database becomes the bottleneck?
If the database is at 95% CPU, I'd add indexes, optimise queries, cache reads, add read replicas, partition or shard, move heavy work to queues and archive old data.
The database is at 95% CPU. You add an index on the slow query, cache repeated reads, add replicas for read traffic, and, later, split data across machines.
What are database indexes and what is the trade-off?

An index is a sorted lookup structure that speeds reads on a column but slows writes and uses space. If a query takes eight seconds, I'd index the fields used in filters and joins, without over-indexing.

An index on email makes 'find user by email' take milliseconds instead of scanning a million rows. The trade-off: every new signup also updates the index, so writes are a little slower and it uses disk space.
What is a push notification system's technical outline?

For push notifications: a device-token registry, a notification service with templates, user preferences, a queue, providers like APNs and FCM, retries and rate limits, deduplication, analytics and opt-out handling. The result is a reliable pipeline.
When a delivery is out for delivery, the system looks up the user's device token, checks they allow notifications, fills the message template, and sends it through Apple's or Google's push service.
Why might one search be slower than another (e.g., email search versus web search)?

Email search is private per-user data with permissions, freshness requirements and small per-user indexes with little cache sharing; web search uses shared, heavily cached and precomputed indexes. Personalisation and access control add cost, which explains the gap.
Web search looks through a huge shared index that can be updated hourly. Email search has a small private index per user, but must be instant (a new email appears in seconds) and respect permissions.
How would you diagnose a connection issue with a social app?

If a user says their music app keeps disconnecting, I'd reproduce by device, network and version, check logs and metrics for errors, timeouts, auth refresh, CDN and regional issues, compare with recent releases, and add retries and better error handling. I'd find the root cause and fix it.
A user says 'my music app keeps disconnecting'. You check whether it's one phone model, one network, or a new app version, look at error logs for that user, and try to reproduce it.
What if a downstream third-party API goes down?

If a payment provider is down, I'd use timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, a fallback provider, queue and retry later, and clear user messaging, while monitoring the provider's status. Customers are protected.
The payment provider is down. Requests time out quickly, a backup provider takes over, and failed payments are saved in a queue to retry later, with a message 'We're confirming your payment'.
What if two users edit the same record at once?

When two users edit the same record, I'd use optimistic locking with version numbers, last-write-wins for simple cases, or merging with operational transforms or CRDTs for collaboration, and show conflicts clearly. The goal is no silent data loss.
Two people edit the same document title at once. With optimistic locking, each edit carries a version number; the second save is told 'This changed since you opened it' and asked to reload or merge.
What if the data centre or cloud region fails?
If a cloud region fails, I'd already be multi-zone and, for critical services, multi-region with replicated data, DNS or traffic failover, regular drills and clear RPO and RTO. Service continues.
A whole cloud region goes down. For critical services you already have a second region ready, with copied data and automatic traffic switching, so users see a brief delay instead of an outage.
What if a bad deployment goes out?

If a bad release goes out, I detect it through monitoring, roll back quickly, and use feature flags, canary releases and automated checks, then write a blameless post-mortem. Knight Capital's 2012 deployment error is a famous cautionary tale.
A new release breaks checkout. Monitoring spots the error rate rising, the team rolls back in minutes, and a feature flag lets them turn the new feature off without redeploying.
How do you handle a hot key (one very popular item)?
If one celebrity post gets millions of reads, I'd cache heavily, replicate the hot item, spread the key with suffixes, use a CDN and rate limit. No single node gets overloaded.
A celebrity posts and millions request that one item, overloading its server. You cache it in many places and keep several copies, so no one machine takes all the traffic.
What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous processing?

Synchronous means the caller waits for the result, which is simple and immediate. Asynchronous means the work is queued and finished later, which is resilient and scalable but needs status handling. Checkout confirmation is synchronous; sending the receipt email can be asynchronous.

Synchronous: at a restaurant counter you wait until your coffee is ready. Asynchronous: you get a buzzer, sit down, and are called when it's done. Sending an email after checkout works the second way, so the customer isn't kept waiting.
How do you secure an API?
I'd use authentication such as OAuth or API keys, authorisation, TLS, input validation, rate limits, logging, secrets management, least privilege and abuse monitoring.
A weather API is secured by requiring a key (who are you), checking what that key may do, encrypting traffic, rejecting malformed input, and limiting each key to 100 requests a minute.
What is OAuth and why does it matter for integrations?

OAuth lets a user grant an app limited access to their account without sharing a password, using access tokens with scopes and expiry, plus refresh tokens. When a customer connects their Google account, I'd request minimal scopes and support revocation.
You tap 'Connect calendar' in a scheduling app. Google asks 'Allow this app to view your events?'. You approve, and the app gets a limited token, never your password, which you can revoke any time.
What is a webhook and how do you make it reliable?
A webhook is an HTTP callback your system sends when an event happens. To make it reliable I'd add signatures, retries with backoff, idempotency keys, dead-letter handling and replay tools.

A payment provider calls your URL when a payment completes. To be reliable you verify its signature, reply quickly, process the same event only once (events can repeat), and keep a retry queue if your server is down.
What is the difference between REST, GraphQL and gRPC (briefly)?

REST is simple, widely used and resource-based. GraphQL lets clients choose fields and reduces round trips, with more server complexity. gRPC is fast and binary, good for internal services. I'd choose by client needs and performance.
REST: ask for /orders/42 and get the whole order. GraphQL: a mobile app asks for just the order's date and total, nothing extra. gRPC: two internal services exchange data quickly in a compact format.
What is data consistency in a payment system, and why is it special?

Payments need strong consistency, atomic transactions, idempotency, an audit ledger, reconciliation with providers and careful handling of timeouts where the state is unknown. Money must be accurate, never lost or doubled.
You transfer ₹1,000 from A to B. Either both the debit and the credit happen or neither does. A unique payment ID prevents double charging, and a daily check compares your records against the bank's.
How do you handle time-sensitive tasks like scheduled jobs reliably?
I'd use a distributed scheduler with locks or leader election, idempotent jobs, retries, and monitoring with alerts for missed runs, so scheduled work is dependable.
A job 'send invoices on the 1st at 9 a.m.' runs on three servers. Without coordination all three send, and customers get three invoices. A lock or a single elected leader makes only one run it.
What are blue-green and canary deployments?
Blue-green runs two environments and switches traffic at once, enabling quick rollback. Canary releases to a small percentage first and expands if healthy. Both lower deployment risk.

Blue-green: two identical environments; you switch all traffic from the old (blue) to the new (green) and switch back if there's a problem. Canary: send 5% of users to the new version first and widen as it proves stable.
How do you migrate a database with no downtime?
I'd replicate to the new database, dual-write or use change data capture, verify consistency, move reads and then writes, keep a rollback, and migrate in stages. That gives zero downtime.

Moving a live database: copy data to the new one while the old keeps serving, keep both in sync, verify they match, switch traffic over in a quiet minute, and keep the old as a fallback for a few days.
What would you monitor for any production system?
I'd monitor the golden signals, latency, traffic, errors and saturation, plus business metrics, logs, traces, alerts with runbooks and dashboards, so issues are noticed early.
For any app you'd watch speed (latency), volume (traffic), failures (error rate) and how full it is (saturation, like CPU at 90%), plus a business signal like orders per minute.
How would you build TinyURL (a URL shortener)?

I'd start by clarifying scale, say 100 million new links a month and a hundred reads for every write. The API is simple: create(longURL) returns a short code, and GET /{code} redirects. I'd generate unique codes by base62-encoding an ID from a counter or ID service so there are no collisions, store code-to-URL in a key-value store, and cache hot links so redirects come from memory. I'd use a 302 redirect if we want click analytics, and send analytics through a queue so it never slows the redirect. Add expiry and abuse checks. The result: redirects in milliseconds, no duplicate codes, and analytics that don't hurt speed.

A user pastes a long link, the system makes a short code (xK9aB2), stores code-to-link, and when someone visits the short link, it looks up the code and redirects. Reads far outnumber writes, so a cache helps.
Design a rate limiter.

A public API is hammered by one client sending 5,000 requests a second and slowing everyone. I'd choose a token bucket, which allows short bursts but enforces a steady rate, keyed by API key, user and IP. Counters live in a fast shared store like Redis with atomic operations, enforced at the gateway. Over the limit we return 429 with a Retry-After header, and limits are configurable per plan. Across regions I'd accept small inaccuracy for speed. Abusers get throttled quickly, normal users are untouched, and the limits are visible and adjustable.
One client sends 5,000 requests a second. The limiter allows 100 per second per client, answers extra requests with 'Too many requests, retry in 1s', and keeps counts in a shared fast store.
Design a notification system.

A retailer wants order updates, promotions and delivery alerts across push, email and SMS without spamming. Services publish events to a queue; a notification service looks up user preferences and quiet hours, applies templates and per-user rate caps, deduplicates, then sends through providers with retries and fallbacks. I'd track delivery and opens, handle opt-outs, and separate critical alerts, like "your delivery is arriving," from marketing. Messages arrive once, on the right channel, and users stay opted in.

A customer's order ships. The system checks their preferences (push on, SMS off), picks the template, sends the push, and avoids sending a promo in the same hour. Failed sends retry, and users can unsubscribe.
Design a chat system like WhatsApp or Slack.

For 50 million users, clients keep a WebSocket connection to a gateway. A chat service assigns message IDs and orders messages within each conversation, stores them in a store partitioned by conversation ID, and pushes to online recipients. Offline users get a push notification and fetch history later. Groups use fan-out through a queue. I'd add delivery and read receipts, presence, media via object storage and a CDN, and end-to-end encryption if required. Messages arrive in order within a conversation and nothing is lost when a phone is offline.
You send 'Hi' on a chat app. Your phone's open connection delivers it to a chat server, which stores it, gives it a sequence number, and pushes it to your friend instantly or when they come online.
Design Instagram.

I'd clarify the features first: post a photo, follow people, see a feed, like and comment. For uploads, the client uploads straight to object storage through a pre-signed URL, a queue triggers resizing and moderation, and a CDN delivers the images. Metadata sits in a sharded database and the follow graph in its own store. For the feed I'd use a hybrid fan-out: precompute feeds for normal accounts, and pull celebrity posts at read time, then rank and cache. Search and notifications are separate services. With replication, caching and monitoring, feeds are fast, uploads are reliable and celebrity accounts don't melt the system.
You post a photo. The image goes to storage, a copy is resized for phones, and your followers' feeds are updated. When a friend opens the app, they see your photo near the top of their feed.
Design an A/B test system (a platform for running experiments).

Five teams run experiments and their results contradict each other. I'd build an experiment config service, deterministic user bucketing by hashing the user ID, exposure logging, a metrics pipeline, a statistics engine for significance, sample size, sequential testing and variance reduction, guardrail metrics, layers so experiments don't interfere, checks such as sample ratio mismatch, and a UI for results and decisions. Teams then decide with consistent methods.

Two teams test the same button at once and get contradictory results. A shared platform assigns each user to a variant consistently, avoids overlapping experiments, and calculates significance the same way for everyone.
What changes when you scale a system from 1 to 100 (users, servers or customers)?
