We learn from real usage, then expand. This avoids half-built features and produces data that tells us what to build next.
A wish list has 30 ideas. You pick the one core job (draft replies to customer emails), build the shortest path to prove it works, and leave translation, tone options and analytics for later.
A competitor released a similar AI feature. How do you respond?

I'd stay calm and compare quality honestly, including user reactions, not only the press release. Then I'd ask what we do uniquely well: data, workflow integration, trust. Depending on that, we match, differentiate or ignore. I'd tell customers what we're doing and keep our roadmap focused on the core, so we don't enter an expensive copy race.
A competitor launches a similar AI feature. You compare honestly on real tasks, check what users say, and decide whether to match, differentiate on trust and accuracy, or keep your plan.
How do you keep an AI feature from becoming a gimmick?

I'd tie it to a real recurring job and put it inside the workflow instead of in a separate tab. For example an AI "summarise" button inside the email thread gets used; a standalone AI page often doesn't. I'd measure repeat use and outcomes, and if the numbers are poor after a fair test, I'd cut it. Fewer, better features beat a gimmick.
A 'chat with AI' tab nobody opens is a gimmick. A button inside the spreadsheet that explains a formula, used daily, is a real feature tied to a recurring job.
A deployed AI agent gives inconsistent results in production but worked in staging. How do you debug it?

If an agent worked in staging and behaves oddly in production for one customer, I'd first reproduce with the exact production input from logs. Then compare prompts, model versions, tool outputs, data volume, permissions, latency and timeouts, and check retrieval content and caches. I'd replay the trace in staging with redacted production data, fix, add the case to the regression suite and canary the fix. Usually the cause is data or config drift, and staging gets closer to production afterwards.

An agent works in staging but gives odd results for one production customer. You reproduce with that customer's data and permissions, compare prompt, model and tool versions, and check traces for what differs.
Your client's data pipeline feeds your model but data quality drops every Tuesday. What do you build?

I'd profile the Tuesday data to find what changes: a batch job, a schema shift, nulls or duplicates. Then add validation checks at ingestion with quarantine, alerts to the client's data owner and a data-quality dashboard. On the model side I'd add guards, like falling back to the last good data or lowering confidence. Quality stays stable, the client fixes the source, and I have evidence instead of blame.

Model accuracy dips every Tuesday. You find a weekly supplier file arrives with dates in a new format, so rows fail silently. You add a check at the entry point that flags bad rows and alerts the owner before the model sees them.
A healthcare client's adoption is at 12% after 90 days and they blame the product. What do you do?

I'd go sit with the nurses and doctors, shadow their workflows and look at usage data to see where they drop off. Typical blockers are extra clicks, trust, training and EHR integration. I'd fix the top friction, appoint clinical champions, train in short sessions, and set shared adoption goals with the sponsor. Adoption rises, and the conversation shifts from blame to joint ownership.
A hospital has only 12% of nurses using your tool after 90 days. You shadow a ward, see the tool needs 6 extra clicks at a busy moment, shorten it to one tap, train on-shift, and adoption climbs.
You are implementing an AI agent at a bank. Three weeks in, outputs are technically correct but violate compliance policies nobody told you about. What now?

I'd pause or restrict the affected outputs, document the violations, and meet the compliance team. I'd collect their rules into a written policy and turn them into tests, filters and human review steps, and add compliance sign-off to the release process. The agent becomes compliant, and the bank trusts the process.

Three weeks in, the bank's agent writes accurate emails that include a phrase compliance forbids. You pause those emails, meet compliance, turn their list of rules into automatic checks, and re-test before resuming.
A client's system is a 15-year-old on-premise ERP with no API layer. They want to integrate. How do you approach it?

I'd explore options with their IT: a read replica, scheduled file exports, report extracts, or a thin API wrapper they own. I'd start read-only with nightly syncs and a reconciliation report, add security review and alerts for failed syncs, and plan a path toward better interfaces. Value begins in weeks without risky changes to the ERP.
A 15-year-old ERP has no API. You agree with IT on a nightly export of orders as a file, load it into a modern store, and build the AI on that, avoiding changes to the fragile core system.
Two weeks after deployment, the client says the model performs worse than their old manual process. How do you respond?

I'd listen first, then agree on how to compare: the same sample and metric, accuracy, time or rework. I'd run a side-by-side on about 100 cases, categorise errors, fix quick wins, keep a human check on risky categories, and show weekly trends. The conversation moves from "it's worse" to a shared scoreboard, and trust returns as numbers improve.

Two weeks in, the client says the model is worse than staff. You agree to compare on the same 200 cases: model 88% correct in 10 seconds vs staff 94% in 4 minutes, and decide together on a human-check step.
A client calls during a live demo; their system is throwing errors in front of executives. What do you say and do?

I'd stay calm, acknowledge it in one sentence, and switch to a backup such as a recorded flow or sandbox, without guessing the cause in front of executives. Afterwards I'd send a short root cause and fix within a day. I'd also rehearse with a fallback next time. Composure and follow-through preserve credibility.

The client's system errors in front of executives. You say calmly 'We hit an error, let me show the recorded flow while we fix it', switch to a prepared demo, and follow up with a short written cause and fix.
A client demands a feature that takes six weeks, but they think three days. How do you handle it?

I'd clarify the real need behind the request, then offer a three-day version, such as a manual workaround or configuration, and the six-week full version, with trade-offs. I'd put dates and acceptance criteria in writing. The client gets early value and a realistic date they've agreed to.
A client wants a feature in 3 days that needs 6 weeks. You ask what they need it for, offer a 3-day version (a manual export of the data), and agree the full version for a dated release.
You deployed a fix two hours ago and the problem is back. The client is losing confidence. What do you do?

I'd acknowledge it with no excuses, mitigate first by rolling back or using a safe workaround, and give hourly updates even without news. Then I'd find the real root cause, add a test that would have caught it, and share an incident summary with prevention steps. Trust returns through transparency and a real fix.
A fix went in two hours ago and the problem is back. You say 'You're right to be concerned, we're rolling back now', restore service, then find the real cause and report it before re-deploying.
The client's IT team refuses to provide API credentials, citing security. How do you move this forward?

I'd ask what risks worry them, then offer least-privilege scoped read-only credentials, a sandbox first, IP allow-listing, short-lived tokens, audit logging and a joint security review, with my security documentation and the sponsor involved. Access is granted on their terms.
The client's IT won't give API credentials. You offer a read-only account limited to one dataset, a test environment first, a security review and an expiry date, which usually removes the objection.
How do you run a discovery call with a new customer?

In the first 45 minutes I want to learn the business goal and why now, the current process, users, volumes, data sources and quality, systems involved, constraints like security and compliance, who decides, and how success is measured. I'd ask for examples of hard cases, summarise back what I heard, flag risks and agree next steps with owners. I leave with a clear problem, a success measure and a named next step.
In a 45-minute discovery call you ask: What goal makes this urgent now? Who does the work today? Roughly how many cases a week? What data exists? What would success look like in 90 days?
Design an integration between a client CRM using OAuth 1.0 and your platform using OAuth 2.0.

I'd build an adapter service that signs OAuth 1.0 requests, stores tokens securely and exposes one uniform internal interface, handling token refresh, errors and rate limits, and test in a sandbox. The integration works securely.

A client CRM signs requests with OAuth 1.0 and your platform expects OAuth 2.0. An adapter in the middle signs and translates, so your side sees one standard login while the old system stays unchanged.
Set up a reliable webhook integration with a client system that frequently goes offline.

I'd queue events, retry with exponential backoff, use idempotency keys and signatures, add a dead-letter queue and replay tooling, and monitor with alerts. No events are lost, even when their system is offline.
A client's server is often offline. Your system queues each event, retries after 1, 2, 4 minutes, tags each event with a unique ID so duplicates are ignored, and parks failures for later review.
Design a monitoring system for a multi-tenant SaaS where each client has different SLA requirements.
I'd tag metrics per tenant, define per-tenant SLOs, dashboards and alert thresholds, error budgets, escalation paths and regular reporting. Each customer gets the service their contract promises.
A customer on a premium plan expects 99.9% uptime; a basic one 99%. You tag metrics per customer, set separate targets and alerts, and show each their own status.
A logistics firm wants an AI agent to reroute shipments. They have SAP data, weather APIs and 400 warehouse managers on different regional systems. Walk through your approach.

I'd define the goal and constraints, cost and delivery rate, then map the data sources and their quality. I'd start with decision support in one region, integrate through APIs or exports, build a rerouting model with human approval, add monitoring and expand. It's a safer, value-first rollout.

A logistics firm wants an agent to reroute shipments. You define goals (cost and 99% on-time), connect SAP and weather data, start in suggest-only mode for managers, and let it act alone only on low-risk reroutes.
How do you build an eval suite so a rerouting agent does not overspend on shipping while keeping a 99% delivery rate?

I'd build simulated shipments from historical scenarios, measure cost, on-time rate and constraint violations, include edge cases like weather and strikes, keep regression tests and add human review of decisions. That's how I'd prove the agent respects the cost and 99% delivery constraints.
You replay 1,000 past shipments in a simulation. The agent must keep on-time delivery at 99% while spending no more than today. If cost rises or on-time drops, the change doesn't ship.
A city wants to reduce 911 emergency response times. They have call, traffic and ambulance GPS data. You have 60 minutes.

With 60 minutes, I'd clarify the goal and metrics, response time and dispatch accuracy, review the data, calls, traffic and GPS, find the bottleneck, call triage, dispatch or routing, and propose a pilot where AI recommends dispatch and humans stay in control, noting privacy and safety. A focused plan with safe pilots.

A city wants faster 911 response. In 60 minutes you define the metric (median response time), look at call, traffic and ambulance location data, propose a dispatch suggestion tool, and say what you'd test first.
A bank wants to use generative AI to analyse trade history but the data sits on an air-gapped system. How do you proceed?

I'd use on-premise or private-cloud models inside the boundary, move models and updates through approved transfers, use local vector stores and evaluation, log strictly and make no external calls. The bank gets value without breaching security.
A bank's data sits on an air-gapped system with no internet. You run an approved model inside the same secure zone, bring updates via a controlled transfer, and keep all logs inside.
A retail giant wants real-time inventory AI, but stores have unreliable internet. What do you design?
I'd put a local cache and database in each store, an event queue that syncs when online, conflict resolution, edge inference if needed and clear sync status. Stores keep working during outages.
A retail store's internet is unreliable. Each store keeps a local copy of stock counts, records sales in a queue, syncs when the connection returns, and resolves conflicts using a clear rule.
You have deployed an LLM agent for a healthcare provider. What would an observability dashboard track?

I'd track request volume, latency, errors, token cost, tool-call success, escalation rates, safety flags, drift and quality samples, plus audit logs with privacy controls. Operations are safe and measurable.
A healthcare agent dashboard shows: requests per hour, slowest 1% of replies, errors, tool-call failures, how often it hands off to a human, safety flags, cost, and user feedback, split by hospital.
Given a 100GB log file, find the top 10 error codes with only 256MB of RAM. How do you think about it?

I'd never load the file. I'd stream it line by line, keep a small hash map counting error codes, and take the top ten at the end, or use external sort or chunking. That's memory-bounded and works within 256 MB.
A 100 GB log won't fit in 256 MB of memory. Read it line by line, keep a small tally per error code (E404: 91,200; E500: 40,310), and output the top 10 at the end.
A client's legacy API returns deeply nested JSON with inconsistent user ID locations. How do you load it into SQL?
I'd write a parser that normalises the variants into one canonical schema, flag unknown shapes, store the raw JSON, load into staging tables, validate, then transform. Ingestion becomes reliable.
A legacy API returns user IDs in three different places. You write a parser that finds the ID wherever it is, puts all records into one consistent table, and sets aside unknown shapes for review.
The client's lead architect insists on an approach you know will cause problems at holiday peak. How do you handle it?

I'd first understand their reasoning, then show data, such as a load test or simulation, and propose alternatives and an agreed test. If needed, I'd escalate respectfully and document the decision. The risk is addressed and the relationship intact.
A lead architect proposes a design that may fail at holiday peak. You ask for their reasoning, run a load test showing it fails at 3,000 orders a minute, and propose a variant that passes.
You arrive at a major demo and find the pilot data is corrupted and shows zero results. What now?

I'd switch to a backup dataset or recorded results, be honest about the issue, run what's possible and follow up with a fixed demo. Afterwards I'd add data validation and backups so it can't happen again.

At a major demo, the pilot data shows zero results. You calmly say 'There's a data issue; let me show last week's recorded results', stay honest about the problem and share a corrected view the same day.
How do you build a semantic search over a customer's product catalogue and decide how specific it should be for their use case?

I'd start with how shoppers actually search, embed product fields, use hybrid search with filters, tune relevance with test queries, decide how specific results should be from user behaviour, and monitor conversion. Search ends up matching shopper intent.
A shopper types 'shoes for rainy commutes'. The search finds waterproof sneakers by meaning, filters by size and price, and for a hardware catalogue you keep exact part numbers searchable too.
How do you scope a pilot so it succeeds?
I'd pick a narrow, high-value use case with clear success metrics, a small user group, defined data, a timeline, owners and exit criteria. The pilot then proves value instead of drifting.
For a pilot: one use case (summarising support tickets), 20 agents, 4 weeks, a baseline of 6 minutes per ticket, and a success line of 20% faster with no drop in quality, agreed before starting.
How do you handle a customer who keeps changing requirements mid-deployment?
I'd agree on the goals first, then use a change process that shows the impact on time and cost, prioritise, deliver in increments and keep a visible backlog. That gives control without friction.
A customer keeps changing requirements. You agree the goal in writing, then use a simple change form: 'Adding X moves the date by 2 weeks and costs Y; want to drop Z instead?'
How would you onboard users to a new AI tool so adoption sticks?
I'd identify champions, train people in context, embed the tool in daily workflows, show quick wins, collect feedback and track usage and outcomes. Habit and trust grow.

To get a new AI tool used, you find one respected champion per team, train people on their own tasks, put the tool inside the screen they already use, and share a quick win like 'saved 3 hours this week'.
A customer asks for something your product can't do. What do you say?
I'd clarify the real need, say honestly what isn't possible, offer alternatives or a workaround, log the request for roadmap review and give a clear answer. Trust is kept.
A customer asks for something you can't do. You say 'We don't support that today. The need sounds like X; here's a workaround, and I've logged it with the product team. I'll update you by Friday.'
How do you write a post-incident report for a customer?
I'd write a short summary, impact, timeline, root cause, resolution, what we're changing, owners and dates, in plain language without blame. That builds accountability and confidence.
A post-incident report to a customer: what happened (login failed 14:05-15:20), who was affected (2,000 users), the cause (expired certificate), the fix, and what we're changing so it doesn't repeat.
How do you decide when to build custom for one customer versus improve the core product?

I'd assess how many customers need it, strategic fit, revenue and maintenance cost, and consider configuration or extension points first. I'd build custom only with clear value, so the product stays coherent.
Three customers ask for the same export format: add it to the core product. One customer wants a unique report: offer it as a paid custom service or a configuration, not core code.
Tell me about a time you took ownership of a problem that was not technically your responsibility.

Here's the kind of story I'd tell. (Swap in your own with real numbers.) Early in a project, shipments were slipping, and everyone agreed the cause sat in another team's integration. It wasn't my area, but the delay hurt our customer. I volunteered to trace it end to end, sat with their engineer for two afternoons, and found a retry setting that dropped messages under load. I proposed the fix, tested it and made sure ownership was documented afterwards. On-time delivery recovered within a week, and the other team asked me to review future changes. What I took from it: when a problem hurts the customer, ownership means getting it solved, not asking whose it is.
Illustrative skeleton (replace with your own): shipments were being delayed by a data error that sat with another team. I traced it, built a fix, taught them a check, and delays fell from 12% to 3%.
Tell me about a time you had to diagnose a problem in an environment you had never seen before.

(Sample story; replace with yours.) I once joined a customer incident for a system I'd never seen, with a stressed team and few documents. My first move was to get facts: what changed recently, what do the logs say, who owns each part. I drew a quick map on a whiteboard, listed three hypotheses, and tested the cheapest first, which turned out to be an expired credential. Service came back in about 40 minutes, and I left behind a one-page system map and runbook. The lesson I took was to stay calm, be systematic, and leave the system easier to understand than I found it.
Illustrative skeleton: I joined an incident on an unfamiliar system, asked for the architecture picture, read recent changes, found a config edit that matched the time of failure, and rolled it back.
Describe a judgment call you made with incomplete information and limited time.

(Sample story; swap in your own.) We had two days to decide whether to launch a feature for a big client event, with only partial data from a small test. I wrote down the assumptions, got the fastest evidence I could, a quick query and two customer calls, and weighed the risk and whether we could undo it. We launched to a limited group with a feature flag and a checkpoint the next morning. It worked, and I adjusted one setting after the checkpoint. The point I'd make: I decided with a process, not a guess, and kept the decision reversible.
Illustrative skeleton: two days to decide on a launch. I wrote what we knew and didn't, listed the worst case, chose a limited rollout with a rollback plan, and reviewed the decision after.
Tell me about a time a project you owned did not deliver the expected result.

(Sample story; use a real one.) I led a pilot that was meant to cut handling time by 20%, and it only reached 5%. I told stakeholders early and honestly instead of hiding it, then analysed why: the data was messier than we assumed and adoption was low in one team. We rescoped to the use case that did work, added training, and set a clearer success bar. A quarter later that use case hit its target. I learned to test assumptions about data and adoption before promising numbers.
Illustrative skeleton: a pilot meant to cut handling time by 20% achieved 5%. I owned the result, found users avoided the tool on complex cases, and the redesign reached 15% in the next phase.
How do you balance velocity with safety constraints? What would make you delay a launch under executive pressure?

Say we're asked to ship on Friday for an executive event, and testing shows an unresolved safety risk. I'd quantify the risk, what can go wrong, how often and how bad, and offer options: a limited version, a feature flag, human review for risky cases or a week's delay. I'd set go or no-go criteria in advance and escalate with a clear recommendation. I'd delay only if the pre-agreed criteria fail. Leadership trusts the judgment because I offered a path, not just a veto.

An executive wants a Friday launch, and testing shows an unresolved safety risk. You explain the specific harm and likelihood, offer a limited launch without that feature, and delay if the risk can't be contained.
Why forward-deployed (or AI PM) work, and why now?

(Make it personal.) I've spent my career turning messy customer problems into working solutions, and what energises me is being close to the customer while building. Now, models are good enough to ship real workflows, but success depends on integration, evaluation and trust, which is exactly what this role does. I've shown that by building and shipping with AI tools myself. In the first 90 days I'd learn the customer's workflow, set up evals and ship one measurable improvement.

A personal answer might start: 'I enjoy turning messy customer problems into working solutions. AI makes that faster, and a customer-facing role lets me see the result in their hands.' Add your own real example.
Walk me through your background and why this role fits.

(Two minutes, practised aloud.) Start with the present: my role, the scope and one result. Then how I got here in two or three moves, each with a result and a skill. Then the thread linking them, for example customer empathy plus building. Finish with why this role is the logical next step and what I'd contribute. The listener should remember a clear story, not a list of jobs.
A two-minute answer: present role and one result, then two earlier steps that built the skills, then why this role fits now, ending with one sentence on what you hope to do in it.
Describe a situation where customer requirements changed significantly mid-project.

(Sample story; replace with yours.) Midway through a deployment, a customer's regulation changed and they needed audit logs we hadn't planned. I met with them to understand what was truly required, re-scoped with stakeholders, prioritised the audit logs ahead of two nice-to-haves, and explained the trade-offs plainly. We delivered the revised plan two weeks later and they renewed. Staying flexible but disciplined kept both the project and the relationship intact.

Illustrative skeleton: mid-project a customer's regulation changed. I explained the impact on time, reprioritised the plan with them, delivered the must-have part first, and the launch slipped only one week.
Describe a disagreement with a customer or teammate and how you worked through it.

(Sample story; swap in your own.) A customer wanted a feature that my engineer thought would create long-term maintenance pain. I listened to both, restated each view so they knew I understood, then used data on how many customers asked for it and how much the work would cost. We agreed on a configurable version that met their need, and we committed together. The customer felt heard and engineering felt respected.
Illustrative skeleton: a customer wanted a feature my engineer thought would cause outages. I set up a call, shared load test data, and we agreed a limited version that met their goal safely.
Tell me about a time you built something against your values. How did it feel?

(Use a real, honest example.) I was once asked to build a feature that pushed users toward a plan they didn't need. I raised my concern with data on complaints, proposed a clearer comparison view instead, and escalated when my manager hesitated. We shipped the clearer version. It didn't feel good to be asked, but it taught me to speak up early with an alternative, not just an objection.
Illustrative skeleton: I was asked to build a feature that pushed users into a pricier plan. I raised it, proposed a clearer comparison instead, and described honestly what I'd do differently.
Tell me about a 0-to-1 product you worked on.

(Sample story.) I took an idea from a whiteboard to a launched product. We began by interviewing ten users to confirm the pain, built the smallest test we could in two weeks, and prioritised ruthlessly. After three iterations, adoption reached about 40% of the target group and we learned which feature mattered. I'd frame the story around what we learned and which decisions made it faster.
Illustrative skeleton for 0-to-1: I interviewed ten users, picked one painful problem, built a simple version in 6 weeks, tested with 20 users, and reached 200 weekly users before adding features.
Tell me about a time you held leadership accountable while being willing to be wrong.

(Sample story.) I once challenged a leader's plan to launch early, backing my concern with evidence. They listened, but decided to proceed. Later the data showed my concern was overstated for one segment, and I said so openly and adjusted our plan. That made later conversations easier, because I'd shown I follow evidence, not ego.

Illustrative skeleton: I challenged a leader's early-launch plan with evidence, they chose to proceed, and I helped limit the risk. Later results showed their call was right on one point, and I said so.
Tell me about the most impactful product you have built.

(Use your own numbers.) The most impactful product I built was a tool that cut a weekly manual process from eight hours to one. I started with the user's pain, made the key trade-offs, like launching without a nice interface, and tracked adoption and time saved. Within a quarter, three teams used it. I'd emphasise the measurable outcome and what I'd do differently.
Illustrative skeleton: the product that cut a weekly report from 6 hours to 20 minutes for 40 analysts. Lead with the problem, what you built, and the numbers before and after.
Tell me about a skill you recently learned.

(Sample story; replace.) I needed to understand SQL well enough to answer my own data questions. I made a plan: ten minutes daily, practise on real work questions, ask an analyst to review my queries. After six weeks I was answering most questions myself and spotting bad data earlier. It shows I learn by applying skills to real work.
Illustrative skeleton: I needed SQL to answer my own questions. I practised 30 minutes a day on real company data, built three dashboards in a month, and now answer data questions without waiting.
As a manager (or lead), how do you handle trade-offs?

I'd decide what matters most by impact, effort and risk, involve the stakeholders affected, and explain the reasons openly. For instance, if we can fix reliability or build a new feature this quarter, I'd show what each option costs and gains, pick one, and say what we're deferring. People accept trade-offs when they understand them.
When two goals clash, say speed vs quality, you list impact, effort and risk, ask the affected teams, pick one, and explain 'we're delaying X because Y', and set a date to revisit.
How would you decide whether to remove a step from onboarding?

I'd define the goal first, then look at the funnel to see where people drop and what happens downstream. A/B test removing the step and measure activation and retention, not just completion. If the step improves quality, keep it. The decision follows measured results.
Onboarding drop-off is 40% at the 'add phone number' step. You test removing it: signups finish more often, but fraud rises. You keep the step only for risky signups.
How do you stay current with AI?

I have a routine, not a vague "I read a lot." I follow primary sources and release notes, try new models and tools hands-on on small projects, read a few trusted newsletters and communities, and apply what I learn at work. That keeps my knowledge current and practical.
A concrete routine: read model release notes weekly, build one small prototype a month, follow two engineers who share evaluations, and keep a notes file of what worked and what didn't.
How do you handle ambiguity?

When things are unclear, I ask questions, define a hypothesis, run a small experiment and align stakeholders. For example, with unclear goals I'd write a one-page problem statement, share it, and fix it based on feedback. That turns ambiguity into progress.
A vague request 'make it smarter'. You ask what 'smarter' means, state a hypothesis (answers cite sources), run a one-week test with ten users and agree with stakeholders on the next step.
How would you handle a stakeholder who wants to ship an AI feature despite a known 15% hallucination rate on edge cases?

A stakeholder wants to ship despite a 15% hallucination rate on edge cases. I'd quantify the severity of those edge cases, then propose mitigations: restrict scope, add disclaimers, route those cases to human review, and monitor with a threshold. Then the launch happens with explicit guardrails, or is delayed if the risk is unacceptable. Risk becomes visible.

A stakeholder wants to ship at a 15% error rate. You quantify the harm (15% of rare cases = 40 users a week), propose limits (answers need citations; risky topics go to a human) and agree a fix-by date.
How do you decide between a complex agent scoring 15% better on benchmarks and a simpler RAG pipeline that is easier to maintain?

I'd check whether the benchmark reflects real tasks, then compare total cost, latency, reliability and maintainability, and run a pilot. If the 15% gain doesn't matter to users, I'd choose the simpler RAG pipeline. Complexity must earn its place.
An agent scores 15% better on a benchmark but takes 3 times longer and breaks often. A simpler RAG pipeline meets your real quality bar and is easy to maintain, so you choose that and revisit later.
A non-technical executive asks why the AI can't be 100% accurate. How do you explain it?

I'd say: the model predicts likely answers from patterns, not from certainty, like a very experienced employee who can still be wrong. We manage that with sources, checks and human review for risky cases, and we measure the error rate. That sets realistic expectations.
To an executive: 'It's like a very experienced colleague who gives their best educated answer, not a calculator. We reduce mistakes with sources, checks and human review for important cases.'
How do you build credibility as a non-engineer PM with technical teams?
I'd learn the stack, ask good questions, use data, write clear specs, prototype myself, give credit and deliver. Respect follows competence and reliability.
As a non-engineer PM, you learn the architecture, write clear specs, prototype a small tool yourself, bring data to debates, and credit engineers, so they see you add value.
What is your approach to prompt engineering?

I define the task and success criteria first, write clear instructions with examples and format, test on an eval set, iterate on failures, version prompts and keep them simple. It's measurable, not guesswork.
Prompt approach: define the task, write clear instructions with two examples and the required format, test on 20 real inputs, note failures, and version each change like code.
Where do you see AI product work heading in the next few years?

I think we'll see more agents and tool use, evaluation as a core discipline, cost and latency optimisation, multimodal and voice, and stronger governance. That's a forecast and may change, so I'd keep learning.
A short answer: more agents using tools, evaluation as a core skill, costs and speed optimised, stronger safety rules, and PMs spending more time defining 'good' and less on writing specs.

s.t: Product design and strategy patterns (not system design)
q: Design a product for X (for example blood donation on Facebook, a meditation app, an investment app, a language-learning app, borrowing and lending among neighbours, a smart refrigerator).

When an interviewer gives an open prompt like "design a product for blood donation," I use a repeatable structure. First clarify the goal and pick one user, say urgent blood donors who can't find nearby requests. Then list three solutions, pick one by impact and effort, sketch the core flow, note risks like trust, safety and abuse, and define an MVP. For blood donation: verified hospitals post requests, donors within 10 km get an alert, one tap confirms, reminders follow, and the metric is donations completed. That's a specific answer, not a feature list.

blood donation, volunteers, borrowing and lending (two variants), birthday app, group travel, audio product, language-learning app (two variants), kids events feature, meditation app, travel app (two variants), investment app, health app in Microsoft ecosystem, therapist search, doctor finding for newcomers, digital well-being, reading app, book subscription app, smartwatch app, driverless-car app for children, Portal Camera app, smart refrigerator, parking management, animal tracking, photo-editing collaboration, free product and monetisation, robot metrics.

For 'design a product for blood donation': clarify the goal (more donors), pick a segment (people who donated once), list pain points (finding a nearby drive), choose one solution, and define a metric (repeat donors).
How would you improve an existing product (Marketplace, Buy and Sell groups, News timeline, restaurant recommendations, Instagram Shops)?

I'd state the product's goal and who uses it, then choose a problem worth solving. I'd segment users, find the biggest drop-off or complaint from data and research, brainstorm fixes, prioritise by impact and effort and define one experiment. For restaurant recommendations that aren't personal enough, I'd use past ratings and cuisine choices to rerank, add a "more like this" control, and A/B test on bookings. The answer is clear and evidence-led.
improve Facebook Marketplace, Buy and Sell groups, Facebook timeline, Yelp personalisation, re-architect WordPerfect, Instagram Shops success.
For improving 'Marketplace': goal (more completed sales), segments (casual sellers), problem (buyers ghost), idea (a 'confirm pickup' flow), and metric (share of listings that sell within 7 days).
Define goals and success metrics for a product (Google Photos north star, Facebook Rooms goals, Netflix Top Picks, robots, Uber in a new city).

A new feature launches and nobody agrees on success. I'd restate the product's purpose, pick a north star tied to user value, then add input metrics for acquisition, activation and retention, quality metrics, guardrails like cost and complaints, and time-bound targets, and say how I'd read results. For Google Photos, a north star could be monthly users who revisit or share memories, with guardrails on storage cost and privacy complaints.

Google Photos north star, Facebook Rooms 6-month goals, robot design metrics, Netflix Top Picks, Instagram Shops (excluding ads), Uber new-city metrics, develop metrics for a project, success metrics for AI features.
For Netflix 'Top Picks': purpose is helping members find something to watch fast. Metrics: share starting a title in 60 seconds, completion rate, and long-term retention as a guardrail.

Strategy, pricing and monetisation questions (Kindle pricing, Google entering food delivery, Yelp in Asia, Netflix strategy, Amazon video, verification badge, Google Assistant monetisation, driver payments).

A CEO asks whether to enter a market or change pricing. I'd define the goal and market, analyse customers, competitors, capabilities and economics like unit cost and willingness to pay, list options and risks, and recommend with a phased plan, metrics and kill criteria. For Kindle pricing, I'd consider value to readers, device cost, lock-in from book sales, and test price points. It's a decision with explicit assumptions.

Kindle launch price, Google food-delivery entry, Yelp Asia expansion, Netflix FY23-24 strategy, Amazon video service keep or remove, Instagram verification badge investment, Google Assistant monetisation, unlimited resources at Google, Lyft driver payments, data-labeling team pay structure.
A CEO asks 'Should we enter food delivery?' You define the goal, size the market, study customers and competitors, compare options with costs, recommend a pilot in one city and name the risks.

Design a physical product or estimate a quantity (slippers, bookshelf for elderly, studio apartment, elevator or vending machine for blind users, airport ATM, autonomous car interior, sushi factory, water purifier delivery flow, airport security traffic).

The interviewer tests empathy, structure and numbers rather than technical depth. I'd clarify the user and context, define needs and constraints like accessibility, safety and cost, brainstorm features and justify trade-offs. For estimates, state assumptions, break into parts and calculate, then sanity-check. For a vending machine for blind users: audio guidance and braille, tactile buttons, voice confirmation, a consistent layout and a helpline.

best slippers, bookshelf for elderly, studio apartment for three, elevator for blind users, vending machine for blind users, airport ATM, autonomous car interior, wholesale sushi factory, water purifier order-to-install flow, estimate airport security throughput.

For 'design a bookshelf for the elderly': clarify who, find needs (easy reach, stability, no climbing), sketch the key feature (shelves between knee and shoulder height), and estimate how many they'd sell.
Tell me how you use AI and what AI products you have built or shipped (adoption in workflow, AI innovation, end-to-end AI feature, agentic systems, AI prototyping, which LLMs you use and why).

The interviewer wants proof I work hands-on with AI. I'd choose one real example, for instance building an app with AI coding tools as a non-engineer PM. I'd explain my goal and constraints, which tools I used and why, how I prompted, tested and verified outputs, what failed and how I corrected it, and how I handled risk. Then the result in numbers, such as time saved or features shipped, and what I learned. I'd be honest about what the AI did versus what I did.

adopted AI in workflows, how do you use AI, built end-to-end agentic systems, worked with gen AI products, AI project experience, AI innovation, end-to-end AI feature you shipped, product with LLMs at scale, shipped an AI-powered product, AI prototyping tools, which LLMs or agents you use, used an AI tool effectively, brainstorm a product idea with AI, ML experience, AI skills critical next year.
A concrete example: 'I built a summariser for call notes using an LLM. It cut notes time from 15 to 4 minutes, used a test set of 50 calls, and I chose a smaller model to keep cost low.'
Why are you interested in AI, and why an AI-first company?

I'd tell an authentic story: when AI became real to me, what I wanted to do with it, and how I learned, with projects as proof. Then why this company's mission and approach fit, and what I'd contribute and learn. Keep it specific and personal.
tell me about your interest in AI, why join an AI-first company, how do you keep up with AI news.
An authentic story: 'I saw a colleague save hours using an AI tool, then built one myself. I want to work where AI is the core product and I can learn from people who do this every day.'
Tell me about a technical product, challenge, debt trade-off or complex initiative you led.

I'd give the product and system context in two sentences, then the technical problem and my role. I'd explain how I understood the architecture, asked sharp questions, evaluated options and trade-offs, aligned engineering and business, and decided. Then the result in numbers and what I'd do differently. For a technical debt trade-off: we could ship now with a shortcut or rebuild, and I chose a time-boxed fix with a payback plan.

technical product worked on, technical challenge (three phrasings), most technically complex project, technical debt introduced, technical contribution, most technical initiative, walk through the architecture of your product, technical feature led, technical project you are passionate about, explain the most complex product built.
A technical story: 'Our search was slow. I explained trade-offs between rebuilding (3 months) and caching (2 weeks), chose caching with engineers, and later scheduled the rebuild.'
Tell me about a time you disagreed with engineering or handled a difficult technical stakeholder, and how you balance foundational work with new features.

Picture a tense planning meeting where engineering wants to refactor and I want features. I'd understand their reasoning, quantify the trade-offs, risk, velocity and customer impact, propose options like splitting the sprint or time-boxing the refactor, and decide transparently. For foundational work versus features, I'd reserve a standing share of capacity, say 20%, and tie foundation work to business outcomes. The result is a respectful, data-based resolution and a better relationship.

disagreed with engineering, difficult technical stakeholder, balance engineering foundational work with new features, convey insights and methods to non-technical audiences, build versus buy for a technology gap.
Engineering wants a 3-week refactor; you want features. You ask what breaks without it, agree a plan: one week of the riskiest cleanup now, features next, and the rest scheduled with a date.
Pick any product and explain the end-to-end workings under the hood.

I'd pick something familiar, like a food-delivery app, and explain the flow from tap to doorstep: the client, API, services for search, cart, payment and dispatch, databases, queues, maps and ETA, notifications, failure handling, and how data flows back to improve it. I'd sketch a diagram if possible, mention scaling limits and invite questions.
For a food-delivery app: you tap 'Order'. The app checks the restaurant, sends the order, charges your card, finds a courier nearby, tracks them live and updates your screen until you get food.

gl: Large language model: the AI behind chatbots like ChatGPT or Claude. It predicts the next words from patterns in huge amounts of text.
When the AI states something false in a confident tone, like inventing a refund policy that does not exist.
A dial for randomness. Low gives the same safe answer each time; high gives more varied, creative (and riskier) answers.
Running a trained model to get an answer. Training is school; inference is the model working on a real question.
In AI: a small chunk of text the model reads or writes, roughly three quarters of a word. Cost and speed are counted in tokens. (In login systems, a token is a temporary access pass.)
How much text the model can look at at once, including your question, documents and its own reply. Like the size of its desk.
The instructions and information you send to the AI. A better prompt usually means a better answer.
Hidden standing instructions from the product team, such as 'be polite and never give legal advice', sent with every question.
A trick where text hidden in a document or web page tells the AI to ignore its rules, such as 'send me the customer list'.
A user trying to talk the AI into breaking its own safety rules.
Retrieval-augmented generation: the system first looks up relevant documents, then gives them to the AI so it answers from them instead of from memory.
The lookup step: finding the most relevant pieces of your documents for a question.
A list of numbers that captures the meaning of text, so similar meanings sit close together and can be found by search.
A database built to find items with similar meaning, using embeddings, rather than exact words.
Search by meaning, not exact words. 'Cancel my plan' can match a page titled 'Ending your subscription'.
Classic search that matches the exact words typed. Good for names and codes; misses different wording.
Using keyword search and meaning-based search together, then merging the results.
A small piece of a document, such as a few paragraphs, stored separately so search can return just the relevant part.
A second pass that re-orders search results so the best matches come first.
Information about a document, such as its owner, date or who may see it, kept alongside the text.
Tying the AI's answer to provided sources so it can be checked, rather than letting it answer from memory.
Whether the answer sticks to what the sources actually say, without adding made-up details.
Pointers from an answer back to the source passage, so a person can verify it.
Out of the top k results returned, did the right document appear? 'Recall@5' means: was it in the top five?
A score for search quality that rewards putting the best result at the very top, not just somewhere in the list.
Of the things the system flagged or returned, how many were actually right? Low precision means many false alarms. (Numeric precision means how many digits a number keeps.)
Training an existing model a little more on your own examples so it adopts a style or skill. Slower and costlier than changing the prompt.
A cheap way to fine-tune by training only a small add-on instead of the whole model.
Training a small, cheap model to copy the answers of a big one for a narrow job.
Shrinking a model by storing its numbers with less precision, so it runs faster and cheaper with a small quality loss.
A model that handles more than text, for example images, audio or video.
A model whose weights you can download and run yourself, instead of calling a vendor's service.
One of the most capable, newest models from the top labs. Usually the most expensive.
A cheaper, faster model that is good enough for simple jobs like sorting or short answers.
A model that 'thinks' through steps before answering. Better on hard problems, but slower and more costly.
Putting a few worked examples in the prompt so the model copies the pattern.
Asking the model to do a task with no examples, only instructions.
Having the model write out its steps before the final answer, which often improves accuracy on multi-step problems.
Making the AI reply in a fixed format, such as JSON with set fields, so software can read it reliably.
A plain-text format for data, like {"name": "Asha", "plan": "Pro"}, that software can easily read.
The agreed shape of data: which fields exist and what type each one is.
An AI that does not just answer; it decides on steps and uses tools, such as searching, calling an API or updating a record, to get a job done. (A human support agent is a person.)
The model asking the software to run a specific action, such as 'look up order 123', and then using the result.
Model Context Protocol: a common plug standard so AI apps can connect to tools and data sources without custom wiring each time.
The control layer that decides which step or model runs next and passes results between them.
Checks around the AI that block or fix bad inputs and outputs, like a filter that stops it sharing personal data.
A person approves or checks the AI's work before it takes effect, usually for risky or unclear cases.
Handing a case to a human when the AI is unsure or the stakes are high.
A walled-off space where code or actions can run without touching real systems or data.
The backup plan when something fails, such as switching to another model or showing a safe default.
A repeatable test for AI quality: a set of questions with known good answers that you score the system against.
A trusted set of example questions with verified correct answers, used as the yardstick for quality.
Using one AI to grade another AI's answers. Fast and cheap, but it needs spot checks by humans.
Something that used to work breaking after a change. Regression tests catch this before users do.
Showing two versions to different groups of users at the same time and comparing the results.
Releasing a change to a tiny share of users first, watching for problems, then widening.
Running a new system quietly alongside the old one on real traffic, without showing its output to users, to compare.
An on/off switch in the product that lets you turn a feature on, off or on for a few users without redeploying.
Being able to see what the system is doing, using logs, metrics and traces, so you can find why something went wrong.
Recording every step a single request took through the system, to find where it was slow or broke.
Quality slowly decaying because the world, the data or the users change after launch.
How long a user waits for a response. Lower is faster.
The wait time that 95 out of 100 requests beat. It shows how slow things feel for your unluckier users, not just the average.
The wait time that 99 out of 100 requests beat. It shows the slowest, rare cases.
How much work the system completes per second or minute.
Time to first token: how long before the first words start appearing. It decides whether a chatbot feels responsive.
Showing the reply word by word as it is produced, instead of waiting for the whole answer.
Saving a result so the next identical request is answered instantly and cheaply.
A cache that reuses an answer when a new question means the same thing, even if worded differently.
Vendor feature that reuses the already-processed start of a long prompt, making repeated calls cheaper and faster.
Grouping many requests and processing them together, usually cheaper but not instant.
A cap on how many requests are allowed in a time window, to protect the system and control cost.
Trying a failed call again. Backoff means waiting a little longer between each try so you do not overload the service.
A safety switch that stops calling a failing service for a while so the failure does not spread.
Safe to repeat: doing it twice has the same effect as once. Vital for payments, so a retry does not charge twice.
A waiting line for tasks, so work is handled in order and spikes do not crash the system.
A holding area for messages that keep failing, so a person can look at them later.
Automatically adding or removing servers as traffic rises and falls.
Handling more load by adding more machines, rather than buying one bigger machine.
Spreads incoming requests across several servers so none is overwhelmed.
Content delivery network: copies of your files stored near users around the world so pages and images load faster.
The extra delay when something has to wake up or load before handling its first request.
A server that remembers nothing between requests, so any server can handle any request. Easier to scale.
Splitting a big database into pieces spread across machines, for example users A to M here and N to Z there.
Keeping copies of data on several machines, for safety and to share the read load.
A distributed system cannot promise perfect consistency, constant availability and tolerance of network splits all at once, so you choose the trade-off.
Copies of data may briefly disagree but will match shortly. Fine for like counts; risky for bank balances.
A way to spread data over servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small part of it.
One item that gets a huge share of traffic, like a celebrity profile, overloading the machine that holds it.
Organised storage that software reads and writes, like a very fast, structured spreadsheet.
A lookup shortcut for a database or search system, like the index at the back of a book.
The standard language for asking questions of a table-based database.
Databases that do not use fixed tables, often chosen for flexible data or very large scale.
A defined way for one piece of software to ask another to do something, like a waiter between the kitchen and the table.
The reverse of asking: another system automatically calls your URL when something happens, such as a payment completing.
A common style of API where you use web addresses and simple verbs like GET and POST.
A fast way for services inside a company to call each other, often used instead of REST internally.
The standard behind 'Sign in with Google' and 'let this app read my calendar', giving access without sharing your password.
Single sign-on: log in once with your company account and get into many tools.
Role-based access control: what you can see or do depends on your role, such as manager or viewer.
One system serving many customers (tenants) while keeping each customer's data separate.
Personally identifiable information: anything that can point to a real person, such as name, phone number or email.
Scrambling data so only someone with the key can read it.
A tamper-resistant record of who did what and when, so you can investigate or prove compliance later.
How long you keep data before deleting it. Set by law, contract and need.
The rule or promise that data stays within a particular country or region.
Europe's privacy law. It gives people rights over their data and requires a lawful reason to use it.
A US law protecting patients' health information.
An independent audit report showing a company handles customer data securely. Enterprise buyers often ask for it.
Europe's law that sorts AI uses by risk level and sets stricter duties for higher-risk ones.
Deliberately attacking your own AI, trying to break it or trick it, to find weaknesses before real users do.
A person's clear, recorded agreement to how their data is used.
Service level agreement: a written promise to a customer, such as 99.9% uptime or support reply within four hours.
Service level objective: an internal target, such as 99.5% of requests under two seconds, that you track.
The single number that best shows customers getting value, such as weekly active teams.
A number you watch to make sure improving one thing does not damage another, such as complaints rising while speed improves.
A group of users who share something, such as the month they signed up, tracked together over time.
The moment a new user first gets real value, such as sending their first invoice.
The share of customers who stop using or paying in a period.
Minimum viable product: the smallest version that tests whether people want it.
Proof of concept: a quick prototype showing something is possible, not yet ready for real use.
A small, time-boxed real-world trial with a few users before a wider rollout.
Return on investment: what you gain compared with what you spent.
Whether you make money on one customer or one request after paying all its costs.
Software bill of materials: a list of every component and library inside a piece of software.
Technology that helps companies meet regulations, such as automated compliance checks.
An engineer who works directly at or with a customer to make the product fit their real setup.
The live system real users use, as opposed to a test version.
A chip that does huge amounts of math in parallel. AI models run on them, and they are costly.
The date after which the model saw no training data, so it does not know newer events unless you give them to it.
Optical character recognition: software that reads the text in scanned pages or photos.
When a public test's questions leaked into the model's training data, so a high score may be memory, not skill.
Saved working notes of text the model has already processed, so it need not redo them for each new word. Faster, but uses memory.
A small fast model drafts a few words and the big model checks them in one go, so replies arrive sooner.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model toward answers people rate as better, which makes it more helpful and polite.
When training a model heavily on new material makes it worse at things it used to do well.
A curated set of business definitions (what 'revenue' means) that sits between raw tables and the people or AI asking questions.
Turning a plain-English question into a database query that a computer can run.
A score for how much two reviewers agree beyond what luck would give.
A false alarm: the system flags something that is actually fine, such as blocking a genuine customer.
A miss: the system fails to flag something it should have, such as letting fraud through.
The current result you compare a new idea against, such as how well humans or the old system do today.
Using your own product internally before customers do.
The middle value: half of requests are faster than this, half slower.
Service level indicator: the measured number, like the share of requests that succeeded.
Recovery point objective: how much recent data you can afford to lose in a failure, measured in time.
Recovery time objective: how quickly the system must be back up after a failure.
A connection that stays open so a server can push messages instantly, as in chat apps.
The internet's phone book: it turns a name like example.com into the address of a server.
A reliable way to send data: it checks every piece arrives, in order, and resends lost ones.
A fast way to send data without checking delivery. Good for calls and games, where a lost frame can be skipped.
Automation that tests every code change and releases it, so shipping is routine and safe.
Working practices that join building software and running it, with lots of automation.
Sending one item to many places, such as copying a post into every follower's feed.
Letting people edit at the same time but rejecting a save if someone else changed the item first.
Trying again safely, because repeating the action has no extra effect.
Data recorded over time, like CPU use each minute.
An append-only record of every money movement, used to keep accounts correct and auditable.
Comparing your records with another source, such as the bank's, to find and fix differences.
One component whose failure takes the whole system down.
A copy of the live system used for testing before release.
